A1A2: On a cold March evening, Iris worked late on an old desk.
Iris fixed old furniture, and she loved her small, quiet workshop.
She had bought the desk at an auction for very little money.
The old wood was dark and scratched, and it smelled sweet.
One drawer was stuck, so Iris pulled it very slowly and gently.
Behind the drawer, there was a small, strange space, and she reached in.
Inside, she found old letters tied together with a blue ribbon.
Every letter was for Daniel Marsh, but nobody had ever posted them.
Iris knew she should not read them, but she opened the first one.
It was from a woman called Ruth, and Iris read until midnight.
Ruth wrote that she came to Saltmere in July with her parents.
Her father was a banker, and he made many strict rules.
One day her watch stopped, so she went into Marsh and Son.
A young man named Daniel fixed it and would not take money.
On Saturday, Ruth tied a blue ribbon in her hair and went out.
At the dance, Daniel asked Ruth to dance, and she stepped on his foot.
They both laughed, and then they talked until the music stopped.
Daniel walked her home along the harbour and showed her the lighthouse.
Iris put the page down and found that she was smiling.
That night Ruth lay awake and listened to the sea.
Daniel showed Ruth his father's workshop, full of clocks of every size.
He taught her how a clock works, and she wound a big one.
One sunny day, they rowed a small boat out to the lighthouse.
They ate sandwiches on the harbour wall and talked about their dreams.
Ruth's mother saw her come home late, but she only smiled.
On a rainy day, Daniel read her a poem in the shop.
Ruth's father had a new job, and the family had to leave.
She told Daniel the sad news at the lighthouse, and he held her hand.
They promised to meet at the station on the seventh of October.
On the seventh of September, the family left, and Ruth watched the lighthouse.
In the city, the Ashbys lived in a tall, grey house.
Ruth asked to visit Saltmere, but her father said no.
On the seventh of October, she sat and watched the clock strike eleven.
Two days later, she wrote her first letter to Daniel at her desk.
The drawer was stuck, so she pulled it out and found a hidden space.
She went to the post office, but she did not buy a stamp.
Every morning, Ruth looked for a letter from Daniel, but none came.
Her father asked a young banker to dinner, but Ruth did not care.
At Christmas, she held a card over the post box, then went home.
On New Year's Eve, she tied her letters together with the blue ribbon.
In spring, Ruth got a job at a small public library.
One night, Ruth's mother said that her father had sent Daniel's four letters back.
Ruth went to her father's door, but she could not knock.
Ruth was afraid that Daniel thought she had sent his letters back.
In 1963, she heard that Daniel had a girlfriend named Margaret.
Then Ruth wrote a last letter and said she had been too afraid.
Iris held the last page, which had old tear marks on it.
Iris sat on the floor and knew she was just like Ruth.
She took her phone and opened a folder of messages she never sent.
The oldest message was to her sister, Pia, from two years ago.
Iris read her old drafts, and every one was brave but never sent.
Two years ago, after their mother's funeral, she and Pia argued about the house.
Pia wanted to sell it, Iris wanted to keep it, and both were angry.
Their mother had taught Iris to love wood, and Iris missed her.
Iris began a message to Pia, but she stopped and went to sleep.
At noon, she looked for Saltmere on the internet and found Marsh and Son.
She called the shop's number, but nobody answered the phone.
She could post the letters, but they were too old for that.
So Iris called Mr Fenn, the man from the auction.
He said the desk belonged to Miss Ruth Ashby, and he would ask again.
Ruth's niece was away, so Iris decided to go to Saltmere.
Early next morning, Iris took a train with the letters in her bag.
An old woman on the train told Iris that nobody visits Saltmere in March.
The woman said not to wait for perfect words, and Iris thought about her drafts.
Then the sea appeared, grey and wide, with a white lighthouse far away.
At Saltmere station, there was one platform and one cold wooden bench.
Iris walked down a steep hill and smelled salt in the wind.
In the harbour, small fishing boats moved up and down on the grey water.
On Quay Street, she stopped at a shop window full of ticking clocks.
A bell rang when she opened the door, and a young man looked up.
He asked if he could help, and Iris asked for Daniel Marsh.
He looked at her carefully and asked her who she was.
Iris took the old letters from her bag and put them on the counter.
The young man, whose name was Jonah, read the address and frowned.
Iris told him about the desk, the drawer and the hidden letters.
Jonah listened, then he turned the sign to Closed and made tea.
He said that Daniel was his grandfather, and his grandmother had died.
Once, his grandfather had told him about a girl who stepped on his foot.
Jonah locked the shop, and they walked along the harbour together.
At the end of the wall, an old man was feeding the birds.
Jonah called out, and the old man turned around slowly.
Daniel had kind eyes, and he smiled warmly at Iris.
When Iris said the name Ruth Ashby, Daniel sat down suddenly.
A crust fell from his hand, and the birds cried loudly.
Later, on a bench, Daniel began to talk about the summer of 1961.
On the seventh of October, he waited at the station for three trains.
Ruth never came, and his four letters to her came back.
Iris gave him the first letter, and he read it aloud.
His voice broke, and Jonah put an arm around his shoulders.
Daniel asked if Ruth was alive, and Iris promised to find out.
There was no train that night, so Jonah found Iris a room.
At dusk, they ate fish and chips on the harbour wall.
They talked about their work, and she learned that he loved clocks.
Then the lighthouse lamp came on and turned across the dark water.
That night, Iris lay awake in her room and listened to the sea.
In the morning, Jonah showed her clocks in pieces in his workshop.
He said that clocks need patience, and Iris said that wood does too.
A clock case was cracked, so Iris showed him how to mend it.
Their hands touched on the clamp, and they both smiled and looked away.
Iris told Jonah about messages she never sent, and he told her to send one.
That afternoon, Mr Fenn called to say that Ruth was alive.
She lived at Harbour View, and Iris wrote the address on her hand.
Iris and Jonah ran to tell Daniel, and he sat down in his kitchen.
Daniel looked at a photo of his wife, Margaret, and he smiled sadly.
He took down the old tin that held his four returned letters.
The next morning, Jonah tied Daniel's tie, and Daniel wore his best jacket.
They drove to Harbour View in Jonah's old blue van.
On the road, Daniel hummed the waltz from the dance.
Harbour View was a white house with a garden full of roses.
In the garden, Daniel stopped and said he could not go on.
Iris went in alone, and a kind nurse pointed to the sun room.
Ruth Ashby sat by a window with a book on her knee.
Iris said her name and held out the letters tied with a scarf.
Ruth saw the blue ribbon and held it against her cheek.
She said the drawer had stuck years ago, and she could not open it.
Then she asked, in a small voice, if Iris knew about Daniel.
Iris said he was in the garden, and Ruth fixed her hair.
Daniel stood in the doorway with his cap in his hands.
Ruth smiled and told him that he was late, and they both laughed.
They sat hand in hand, and Ruth read her last letter aloud.
In the garden, Jonah said he had never seen his grandfather so young.
Jonah asked what her own letter was waiting for.
Iris took out her phone and wrote a short message to Pia.
She pressed send, and her heart beat very fast.
They walked around the roses while she waited for an answer.
Pia answered at once, and Iris read her message twice.
Iris laughed and cried, and Jonah gave her a clean cloth.
They talked on the phone, and both of them said sorry.
Ruth said she had been afraid, and Daniel said he never forgot her.
Ruth asked Iris to finish the desk and bring it to her.
Visiting time ended, and Daniel promised to come back on Saturday.
On the drive home, Daniel fell asleep, and he was smiling.
Jonah asked Iris to dinner, and she said she could be persuaded.
At his gate, Daniel hugged Iris and thanked her many times.
Jonah walked Iris up the hill under the light of the lighthouse.
Next morning, Jonah waited on the platform and waved as her train left.
On the train, Iris leaned on the window and smiled all the way.
At home, she began to restore the old desk in her workshop.
Every evening, Jonah called her, and they talked about their days.
She fixed the secret drawer first, so that it would never stick again.
She found the letters R and A cut into the wood under a drawer.
On the top, there was a faint ring of old ink, and she left it.
Jonah called and said Ruth had read Daniel's four old letters.
One Saturday, Pia came to the workshop with a big cake.
The sisters sat on the sofa, drank tea and talked about the house.
Pia said she was afraid, and Iris said she missed their mother.
They agreed to sell the house, and to keep their mother's chair and tools.
Pia listened to the story of the desk and wiped her eyes.
In the third week, Iris waxed the desk, and the room smelled of lavender.
Then Jonah stood in the doorway holding a small walnut clock.
Jonah hung the clock on her wall, and it began to tick.
He said it was for her, and he looked very nervous.
He asked her to dinner, so she changed and brushed her hair.
They went to a small restaurant with candles on every table.
Over dinner, Jonah took out an old letter and gave it to her.
Iris read it slowly, and it said that she made him brave.
She stood up and kissed him, and everyone around them smiled.
The waiter brought a pudding with two spoons and a small candle.
They walked home in the rain under one umbrella.
At her door, she told him that she was glad he had come.
On Saturday, they wrapped the desk in blankets and carried it out.
They drove along the coast road with the desk behind them.
Daniel waited at Harbour View with a bunch of yellow flowers.
Four people carried the desk into Ruth's sunny room.
Ruth touched the old ink ring and smiled with wet eyes.
Iris showed her the secret drawer, and it opened smoothly and quietly.
Daniel gave Ruth new paper, new envelopes and a book of stamps.
Ruth wrote a letter to Daniel, and Daniel wrote one to Ruth.
They posted both letters in the red box at the gate.
Ruth waved from her window, holding the old blue ribbon.
In April, Ruth said she wanted to live in Saltmere again.
Jonah found a small white cottage near the lighthouse.
Ruth packed her books, her glasses and the old biscuit tin.
Moving day came in May, and Jonah drove her along the coast.
She walked slowly along the harbour wall to the lighthouse.
The desk stood under the window, and Ruth wrote her first letter there.
She visited Marsh and Son, and the little brass bell rang.
Ruth told Iris that she had been a librarian for forty years.
Her one sad memory was a letter, and she gave Iris her old pen.
She told Iris not to keep her words in a drawer.
In June, Iris's landlord said her workshop lease would end in September.
Pia told her to go to Saltmere, because there she was happy.
In Saltmere, Iris saw an empty shop on Quay Street.
Mr Pascoe unlocked the door and showed her the empty rooms.
The light was perfect, so Iris said she would take the shop.
That evening, Jonah lifted her off her feet and spun her round.
Jonah painted a sign for her new shop, and Daniel watched.
In August, there was a dance in the village hall.
Ruth wore her blue ribbon, and she danced slowly with Daniel.
Jonah stepped on Iris's foot, and they both laughed.
On a warm evening, the four of them sat on the harbour wall.
Ruth read aloud a letter from Daniel that had come in the post.
Iris said she must go to the city one more time to pack.
In the city, Pia helped her pack up the old workshop.
That evening the van was full, and the workshop was clean and empty.
Iris sat at the empty bench with Ruth's pen and a clean page.
She wrote the words that she had never dared to say.
She sealed the letter, wrote Jonah's name and put a stamp on it.
She walked down the dark street to the red post box.
She let the letter go, and it fell into the post box.
B1B2: Iris Calloway restored old furniture for a living, and she loved nothing more than a piece with a story. On a cold evening in March, she stayed late in her workshop to begin work on a battered oak desk.
Her workshop was a long, cold room full of clamps, chisels and tins of wax, and she knew where everything was. Iris liked it that way, because tools, unlike people, always did exactly what she asked.
She had bought the desk at an auction three days earlier, and nobody else had wanted it. Mr Fenn, the auctioneer, had sold it to her for a price so small that he looked almost embarrassed.

The oak was dark with age and scarred by generations of elbows, but it still smelled faintly of lavender. Iris ran her thumb along the edge and felt that, like all old things, it was waiting to tell her something.
One of the drawers was stuck fast, and no amount of pulling would move it. Iris fetched a thin blade and spent half an hour coaxing it, until it slid out with a long, tired groan.

The space where the drawer had been looked far too shallow for the size of the desk. Iris frowned, switched on her torch and slid her hand into the dark gap, where her fingers touched something soft and papery.

Behind the drawer lay a bundle of letters tied with a faded blue ribbon, more than thirty of them. Every envelope was addressed to a man named Daniel Marsh in a place called Saltmere, and not one had ever been posted.

Iris knew that private letters were not hers to read, and she held the first envelope for a long time. In the end, her curiosity was stronger than her good manners, and she carefully unfolded the page.
The letter was dated the ninth of October, 1961, and the ink had faded to the colour of weak tea. It began, “Dear Daniel, I am writing this although I know I will never send it.”
Iris read to the end, where the writer had signed herself simply Ruth, and then she began another. By the time the workshop clock struck midnight, she had forgotten her tea and the cold.

In a later letter, Ruth went back to the summer of 1961, when her family arrived in Saltmere at the end of July. Her father, a banker, was waiting for a new post, so he rented a grey house above the harbour for the summer.

Her father had rules for everything, from the hour she rose to the books she was allowed to read. For two weeks Ruth walked alone along the harbour, bored and a little angry, with nobody to talk to but the gulls.
Then, in the middle of August, her wristwatch stopped, and she noticed a clock shop on Quay Street. The sign above the door said Marsh and Son, and the bell rang loudly as she pushed the door open.

Behind the counter stood a young man who opened the watch with tiny tools and mended it in minutes. When she reached for her purse, he shook his head and asked if she would like to come to the dance on Saturday.
On Saturday evening, Ruth told her parents she had a headache and went to her room. She slipped out through the kitchen door, tied a blue ribbon in her hair and ran down the hill to the village hall.
The hall was hung with paper lanterns, and a small band was playing a slow waltz. Daniel asked her to dance, and Ruth, who had never danced with a boy before, trod on his foot at once.

Daniel only laughed and said that his foot had been through worse, and soon Ruth was laughing too. They stood by the open door talking until the band packed up, and she told him things she had never told anyone.

Daniel walked her home the long way, along the harbour wall, and showed her the white lighthouse at the end. He told her proudly that its lamp had never once failed, not even in the worst storm his father could remember.

Iris put the page down and found that she was smiling, which surprised her, because it was after one in the morning. She had never met these two people, but she already hoped, against all the evidence, that nothing would go wrong.
That night Ruth lay awake in the attic bedroom, listening to the sea. She wrote that she had never felt so awake in her whole life, and that she could still hear the waltz.

Daniel took her upstairs to the workshop, where thirty clocks ticked on every wall and shelf. His father, old Mr Marsh, looked up from his bench, nodded kindly and went back to a tiny wheel without a word.

He showed her how the spring pulls, how the wheels turn and how a small lever lets time escape, one tick at a time. “A clock is just patience made into a machine,” he said, and Ruth thought she had never heard anything so wise.

One bright morning they borrowed a small blue boat and rowed out towards the lighthouse rocks. Daniel let Ruth take the oars, and she laughed so much at her own splashing that they went round in a circle.

Almost every day they ate their sandwiches on the harbour wall, with the gulls watching for crumbs. Daniel said he would be a clockmaker like his father, while Ruth said she only knew she did not want her father's plan.
Ruth came home later each evening, with salt in her hair and her shoes in her hand. Her mother noticed, of course, but she only smiled and said nothing, and Ruth loved her for it.

One wet afternoon they sat in the shop with the rain running down the window, and Daniel read her a poem he had copied out. Ruth told him her secret ambition, which was to go to university, and he said he had never doubted she would.

At the start of September, her father came home with a letter from his bank, and with some gossip from the town. The family would leave on the seventh, he said coldly, and she would not speak to the clockmaker's boy again.
She told Daniel at the foot of the lighthouse, with the wind pulling at her hair. For a long time neither of them said anything, and then Daniel took her hand and promised to write every week.

Daniel made her promise that she would come back for one day, on the eleven o'clock train on Saturday the seventh of October. He said he would be on the platform with his best jacket on, and Ruth swore that nothing in the world would stop her.
On the seventh of September, the car was packed, and her father counted the suitcases twice. Ruth looked back through the rear window until the white lighthouse shrank to a pin and the hill hid it.

The Ashbys' new home was a tall, grey house in the city, with iron railings and a dark front hall. Her father had decided that Ruth would take a course in typing and bookkeeping, and that she would begin the following week.

Ruth waited three weeks and then asked her father, as politely as she could, if she might visit Saltmere for one day. He did not even look up from his newspaper, and he said that the boy would have forgotten her by Christmas.

On the seventh of October, her father sent her and her mother to visit a distant cousin. Ruth sat stiffly in a stranger's drawing room, and when the clock struck eleven, she closed her eyes and saw Daniel on the platform.

On Monday night, Ruth sat at the oak desk her father had bought for her studies and began to write. The letter was long and angry and ashamed, and when she had finished it, she knew that she could not possibly post it.

She tried to hide it in a drawer, but it stuck, so she pulled it right out and found a hollow space behind it. The space was just big enough for a bundle of letters, and she felt that the desk had been waiting for her secrets.

On Wednesday she copied Daniel's address onto an envelope, put on her coat and walked all the way to the post office. She stood in the queue for ten minutes, and then, when she reached the counter, she turned around and went home without buying a stamp.
Every morning she waited in the hall for the post, and every morning there was nothing for her. By November she had stopped hoping, and on a foggy night she wrote a second letter instead.

Her father invited a young banker called Mr Whitlock to dinner, and Ruth could see exactly what he was planning. She was polite and she was silent, and when Mr Whitlock asked what she liked to read, she said, “Mostly letters.”

At Christmas, snow lay on the pillar box at the end of the road, and Ruth stood before it with a card. She held it over the slot for so long that her fingers went numb, and then she put it back in her pocket.

On New Year's Eve, as the church bells rang, Ruth tied the letters she had written together with her blue ribbon. She promised herself that she would post them all soon, and she hid them away behind the drawer.

In the spring of 1962, Ruth finished her course and, to her father's annoyance, took a job at a small public library. She wrote that she was happier among the shelves than she had been all winter, and that every month she wrote Daniel another letter.

One night in the kitchen, her mother finally told her the truth, with tears running down her face. Daniel had written four letters that autumn, and her father had sent every one of them back unopened.

Ruth ran upstairs, then down again, and stood outside her father's study with her hand raised to knock. She stood there until the clock in the hall struck midnight, and then she went to bed without making a sound.
She wrote in her next letter that Daniel must think she had sent his letters back herself. Every month she waited made it harder to post anything, and she no longer knew what to say after so long.
In the winter of 1963, a friend of her mother's sent news from Saltmere. The clockmaker's son was walking out with a kind girl named Margaret, and the whole town expected a wedding.
In the spring of 1963, Ruth wrote her last letter to Daniel. She said she was glad that he was happy, and she admitted that she had been too frightened to post a single one of them.
Iris read the last letter twice, and her hands shook, because the paper was spotted with the marks of old tears. Its final line was so simple and so brave that she had to put a hand over her mouth.
Outside, the sky was turning grey, and the first birds were singing. Iris sat in the sawdust with the letters beside her, knowing she was no better than Ruth at saying what she felt.
She picked up her phone and opened a folder that she had never shown to anyone. It held dozens of messages, written late at night in careful words, and not one of them had ever been sent.
There were messages to old friends, to a landlord and to a teacher she had once admired. The oldest, from two years ago, began, “Pia, I am sorry about the house,” and it still sat there, unsent.
By the time the sun was fully up, Iris had read every draft in the folder. They were kind, brave and honest, and every one of them had been quietly abandoned.
After their mother's funeral, Iris and Pia had stood in the hall of the house on Pell Road, among the boxes. They had meant to sort her things quietly, but the quiet had not lasted.

Pia wanted to sell the house at once, because she needed the money and could not bear to see it empty. Iris wanted to keep it exactly as it was, and each of them said things that could not be taken back.

Their mother had been a carpenter's daughter, and she had taught Iris to love wood, sandpaper and patience. Her little wooden plane still sat on the workbench, and some evenings Iris picked it up just to feel its weight.
She wrote a new message to Pia, deleted the first line and wrote it again. Then her tired eyes closed, and she lay down on the old sofa in the corner and slept for three hours.
At noon she woke with a stiff neck and one thought, and she searched online for Saltmere. To her surprise, a plain little website showed a shop on Quay Street still called Marsh and Son.
The website gave a telephone number, and Iris dialled it before she could lose her nerve. It rang and rang in what she imagined was a dusty shop full of clocks, but nobody answered.

She could simply post the letters, she thought, but sixty-five years was far too long for a stamp to mend. These words had waited long enough, and they ought to be put into the right hands by somebody who cared.
She remembered Mr Fenn's card in her pocket and rang the auction house. When he answered, she explained, in a rush, that she had found something in the desk.

Mr Fenn said the desk had come from the flat of a Miss Ruth Ashby, whose niece had cleared it. He promised to ask the niece what she knew, and he said it was the most romantic telephone call of his career.

That evening Mr Fenn telephoned to say that Ruth's niece was away until Monday and could not be reached. Iris looked at the letters on her bench and decided, at last, to stop waiting and take them to Saltmere herself.
Early the next morning, she wrapped the letters in a scarf and caught the first train. The carriage was cold and almost empty, and the sky outside was the colour of an old coin.
Opposite her sat an old woman with a ball of green wool, who asked where she was going. She laughed kindly and said that nobody goes to Saltmere in March, except for love or for funerals.

Iris said that it was a little of both, and the woman nodded as if that were the most sensible answer in the world. “Do not wait for the right words,” she said, going back to her knitting, “because they never come.”

After two hours the land fell away, and the sea appeared, wide and grey and shining under the clouds. Far along the coast, small and white against the sky, Iris saw a lighthouse, and her heart gave a strange little jump.

The train stopped at a tiny station with one platform, one wooden bench and a clock that had stopped at ten past four. Iris stepped down, shivering in the wind, and thought of a young man in his best jacket who had once waited there.

She followed a steep lane down between slate roofs and crooked chimneys, with the smell of salt growing stronger at every step. Washing flapped in small gardens, and a cat watched her from a wall, as if it had been told to expect her.

At the bottom of the hill lay the harbour, where fishing boats rocked on the grey water and gulls cried overhead. At the end of a long stone wall stood the lighthouse, white and tall and exactly as the letters had described it.

Quay Street ran along the water, and halfway down it she found a narrow shop with a faded green sign. The window was crowded with clocks of every size, and she stood there for a minute, trying to feel brave.

At last she pushed the door, and a little brass bell rang over her head, exactly as it must have done for Ruth. Behind the counter a tall young man looked up from a watch he was mending, and he did not smile.

The young man took the lens from his eye and asked, a little stiffly, whether he could help her. Iris had practised her speech on the train, but now she could only say that she was looking for Daniel Marsh.
He did not answer at once, and she could see him weighing her up. “Strangers have come before,” he said at last, “and they were not all honest, so you will forgive me for asking who you are.”

Iris did not know where to begin, so she unwrapped her scarf and laid the bundle of old letters on the counter. The blue ribbon had come undone on the train, and the envelopes slid across the glass like leaves.

The young man bent over the nearest envelope and read the address, while Iris explained that a woman named Ruth Ashby had written every one. He said that he was Jonah Marsh, that Daniel was his grandfather, and that he had never heard of any Ruth Ashby.

So Iris told him everything: the auction, the stuck drawer, the hidden space and the thirty letters that had never been posted. As she spoke, the suspicion slowly left his face, and he began to look at her with a puzzled kind of wonder.

When she had finished, Jonah crossed the shop, turned the sign on the door to Closed and filled an old kettle. “Marsh and Son has stood here for a hundred years,” he said, “and I have never once closed it for lunch.”

Over tea, he explained that Daniel was his grandfather, and that his grandmother Margaret had died six years ago. He pointed to a photograph beside the till, of a smiling woman in a garden, and his voice was very gentle.
“Grandad rarely talks about the old days,” Jonah said, “but once he told me of a girl who trod on his foot.” Iris felt the hair rise on her arms, because she knew that story by heart.

Jonah locked the shop, tied the letters back into her scarf and walked beside her along the harbour. He was a quiet man, and he talked mostly about clocks, as if the ticking made the silences easier to bear.

At the end of the long wall, an old man in a patched coat was throwing crusts to a crowd of gulls. “That is Grandad,” said Jonah, and his steps grew slower, as if he suddenly wondered whether this was a kindness.

Jonah called out, and the old man turned slowly, his white hair blowing across his forehead. He was thin and a little bent, but his eyes were bright and kind, and he looked at his grandson with obvious pleasure.
Daniel shook Iris's hand with old-fashioned courtesy, and he teased Jonah for leaving the shop on a working day. “Visitors at the end of the wall,” he said, “and the gulls will be jealous.”
Iris took a deep breath and said, “Mr Marsh, I think you knew a girl called Ruth Ashby.” The crust fell out of Daniel's hand, and he sat down very suddenly on the stone wall.

For a long time he said nothing, and the gulls screamed above him as the waves slapped against the wall. When he asked how she knew that name, Iris sat beside him and gently explained about the desk and the letters.
Jonah led them to a bench out of the wind, and Daniel sat with his hands on his knees. He had never told his grandson the whole story, he said, and he thought that it was time.

He told them that in 1961 he had met a girl who trod on his foot, and that he had never been so happy. On the seventh of October he waited on the platform in his best jacket, but she was not on any of the three trains.
He wrote four letters to the address on the ticket, and every one came back unopened, with Return to Sender written across it. Daniel decided that she had changed her mind, and he wrote no more.

Iris untied her scarf and gave him the first letter, the one dated the ninth of October, 1961. Daniel put on his glasses with trembling fingers, and he began to read aloud, very slowly, the words that had waited so long.

At the line about the clock striking eleven in a stranger's drawing room, his voice cracked and stopped. He took off his glasses and wept openly, and Jonah sat down beside him and put an arm around his thin shoulders.
When Daniel could speak again, he took both of Iris's hands and asked, “Is she alive?” Iris said she did not know, but that she would find out, and she promised it as the sun sank into the sea.

There was no train back until the morning, so Jonah took her to Mrs Dunmore's guesthouse on the hill. Mrs Dunmore, a large and cheerful woman in a flowered apron, gave her a small room with a window full of sea.

At dusk Jonah arrived with two parcels of fish and chips, and they ate them on the harbour wall with their legs over the edge. A bold gull snatched a chip from Iris's hand, and for the first time that day Jonah laughed out loud.

He said he had learned the trade from his grandfather, and that he had once dreamed of leaving Saltmere but never had. Iris said that she had learned hers from her mother, and that she had never once felt the wish to leave a workbench.

As the light faded, the lamp in the lighthouse came on, and a long white beam began to sweep slowly across the water. Jonah said that his grandfather had taught him to love that light, because in all the years it had never once failed.

Back in her little room, Iris lay awake with the window open and listened to the waves on the harbour wall. She found herself thinking about the sister she had not spoken to for two years, and about a quiet man with a deep laugh.

In the morning Jonah took her up the narrow stairs to his workshop, where trays of tiny wheels and springs lay under lamps. There were clocks in pieces on every bench, and Iris felt as if she had entered a very small, orderly city.

Jonah held a spring finer than a hair in a pair of tweezers and said that his work was mostly waiting. Iris smiled and told him that hers was the same, because you cannot hurry wax or glue or old wood.

A walnut clock case lay cracked on the bench, and Jonah sighed, because he did not know how to mend it. Iris looked at it for a moment, rolled up her sleeves and asked for wood glue, a clamp and a cloth.

She showed him how to work glue into the crack with a thin blade and how to tighten the clamp slowly and evenly. Their hands met on the clamp, and they both stopped, looked at each other and then at the wall, and said nothing at all.

While the glue dried, Iris found herself telling him about the messages on her phone that she wrote and never sent. Jonah listened carefully, and then he said, quite gently, that she should send the one to her sister.
That afternoon, while the glue was still drying, Iris's phone rang, and it was Mr Fenn. He had spoken to Ruth's niece, he said, and Ruth Ashby was alive, eighty-four years old and as sharp as a tack.

Ruth lived in a care home called Harbour View, about two hours' drive from Saltmere, and Mr Fenn read out the address twice. Iris had no paper, so she wrote it on the back of her hand with the black pen from Jonah's bench.

She and Jonah hurried to Daniel's small cottage behind the harbour, where he was peeling potatoes at the kitchen table. When he heard the news, he put down the knife, wiped his hands on a tea towel and sat very still.

On the mantelpiece stood a photograph of Margaret, laughing in a summer hat, and Daniel looked at it for a long time. “She knew about Ruth,” he said, “and she never minded, because she said that everyone should keep a window open in their heart.”

He was afraid, he confessed, that Ruth would be a stranger now, and that he would be a stranger to her. Then he went upstairs and came back with an old biscuit tin that held his four returned letters, still sealed.
The next morning Daniel put on his best jacket and combed his white hair flat with water, just as he had at the station. Jonah tied his tie for him, because his hands would not stop shaking.

Jonah's old blue van smelled of oil and sandwiches, and it rattled along the coast road with all three of them squeezed into the front. The sea flashed on their left, and the sky was a washed, pale blue, as if the whole morning had been cleaned for the occasion.

To steady his nerves, Daniel began to hum a slow waltz, tapping the rhythm on his knee with one finger. After a few bars, Iris closed her eyes and listened, and Jonah, who did not know the tune, drove a little more slowly.
Harbour View was a long white house on a hill above the sea, with a wide rose garden at the front. The bushes were still bare, with the first red leaves of spring just breaking from the stems.
Halfway along the gravel path, Daniel stopped, and the hand that held the biscuit tin began to shake. “I cannot go in,” he whispered, “because what if she does not want to see me?”

Iris left the two men by the roses and went in alone, with her heart thumping in her ears. At the front desk a kind young nurse looked at the address on her hand, smiled and pointed her towards the sun room.
The sun room was warm and bright, with tall windows and a row of armchairs. In the last chair, by the window, a small, upright woman with white hair sat reading a library book.

Iris crossed the room, asked, trembling, whether she was Miss Ruth Ashby, and held out the bundle of letters. “I have been for eighty-four years,” said the woman, looking at the bundle in Iris's hands, “and who might you be?”

The old woman looked at the blue ribbon, faded to the colour of a winter sky, and every drop of colour left her face. Then she took it, pressed it against her cheek and began to laugh and cry at the same time.

The drawer had stuck fast the very day she hid the last letter, she said, and she had never managed to open it again. She had never asked anyone for help, because she was too ashamed, and when she moved here, her niece had sold the desk by mistake.
“Please tell me one thing,” she said, and her voice became very small. “Do you know, by any chance, what became of Daniel Marsh?”

Iris knelt beside her chair and said that Daniel was in the garden, holding a tin of letters of his own. Ruth smoothed her hair and her cardigan with fingers that would not keep still, and said that somebody had better fetch him quickly.
Iris ran out to the roses and brought Daniel in, one hand under his elbow. He stopped in the doorway of the sun room, cap in both hands, like a boy who has been sent for by the headmaster.
Ruth looked at him across the long room, at the white hair and the kind eyes that had not changed. “You are late,” she said, in a voice that shook, and then they both began to laugh.

He crossed the room, sat down beside her and took her hand, and for a while neither of them said a word. Ruth read her last letter aloud, and at its last line Daniel whispered, “I came as fast as I could.”

Iris and Jonah stood in the rose garden, looking at the sun room window, where two white heads were bent together. “I have never seen him look so young,” said Jonah, and his voice was not quite steady.

They stood without speaking for a while, and then Jonah asked, a little shyly, what her own letter was waiting for. Iris felt the question land somewhere under her ribs, and she took her phone out of her pocket.
She opened the draft to Pia, and this time she did not read it through. She cut the long apology down to three plain lines: she was sorry, she missed her sister, and she hoped they could talk.

Her thumb hovered over the button for what felt like an hour, while a blackbird sang in the rose bushes. Then she pressed send, and the little message flew away with a soft sound, and she felt sick and light at the same time.
They walked slowly round the rose beds, and Jonah, to distract her, told a story about a customer whose clock ran backwards. Iris did not hear a word of it, but she was grateful for every one.
Her phone buzzed before they had even finished the second circuit of the roses. Pia answered at once: “I have waited two years for this, so please call me, because Mum would be glad.”

Iris read it twice, and then a laugh came out of her that turned halfway into a sob. Jonah, who had been standing very politely a few steps away, produced a clean handkerchief that smelled faintly of clock oil.
She rang her sister straight away, and for a few seconds neither of them could speak. Then Pia said her name, and they both began to say sorry at the same moment, and then they both began to laugh.

When Iris and Jonah came back, Daniel had given Ruth the biscuit tin, and she held one of the sealed envelopes in her lap. She told him why she had never posted her letters, and he said very simply that he had never forgotten her, not for one day.
She was glad, Ruth added, that he had married Margaret, who sounded like a very good woman. Then she turned to Iris and asked whether she would finish restoring the desk and bring it to her.

When visiting time ended, a nurse came in with a trolley and a polite cough, and Ruth looked at the clock with real dismay. Daniel promised to come back on Saturday, and the Saturday after that, and every Saturday for as long as they would let him.
It was dark by the time they drove away, and the headlights swept along the empty coast road. Daniel fell asleep against the window with his cap in his lap, and he was smiling like a boy.

Jonah watched the road for a long time, and then he asked, very quickly, whether she would have dinner with him in the city. She pretended to think about it for a while and said that she could probably be persuaded.

They stopped at Daniel's gate under the streetlamp, and Jonah helped his grandfather out of the van. Daniel took Iris's face in his old hands, kissed her on the forehead and thanked her three times, as if once would never be enough.

Jonah walked her up the hill to Mrs Dunmore's in the dark, and every few seconds the lighthouse beam swept over them and moved on. At the blue door he said goodnight, and neither of them knew quite what to do with their hands.
The next morning Jonah stood on the platform to see her off, and the wind blew his hair into his eyes. “I shall ring every evening,” he said, “and I am not going to be late.”

As the train pulled out, Iris leaned her forehead against the window and watched the little station shrink to nothing. It was only when a man across the aisle smiled at her that she realised she had been smiling all along.
Back in the workshop, she stood the oak desk under the lamp and began to strip away the old polish. This was the part of her work that she loved best, because it felt like listening.

Every evening at seven, her phone rang, and it was Jonah, with the sound of the clocks ticking behind him. They talked about everything and nothing, about his customers and her varnish, and neither of them ever wanted to be the first to say goodnight.

The secret drawer was the first thing she mended, and she took more care over it than over the rest. She planed the runners, waxed them and slid the drawer in and out a dozen times, until it moved as quietly as a breath.

Under a drawer, in a corner that no polish had reached, Iris found two small letters cut into the wood: R and A. Beside them someone had scratched a tiny heart, and then plainly thought better of it and tried to rub it out.

On the top of the desk, the stripped wood showed a pale ring of ink where a bottle had stood for years. Iris could have sanded it away in a minute, but she looked at it for a while and decided to leave it.

On Saturday night Jonah told her over the phone that Ruth had read Daniel's four old letters at last. They were short, shy and tender, he said, and each of them began with the words Dear Ruth, I hope you are well.

On the second Saturday, a car pulled up outside the workshop, and Pia climbed out with a large cake tin held in both arms. She stood in the doorway, looking nervous, and said that she had not known what else to bring.

The sisters sat on the old sofa with tea and large slices of cake, and for a while they talked about nothing in particular. Then Pia put down her fork and said that she wanted to talk about the house, and the room went very quiet.

Pia admitted that she had been frightened about money, and that she had hidden her fear behind a quarrel. Iris admitted that she had refused to listen, because she could not bear to lose Mum a second time.
They agreed at last that the house should be sold and the money shared fairly. They would keep their mother's chair, her tools and the old kitchen table, and spend one last weekend there together.

Pia wandered over to the desk, which stood half finished under the lamp, and Iris told her the whole story from the beginning. By the end of it, Pia was wiping her eyes with a paper napkin and saying that she wanted to meet them both.

In the third week, Iris rubbed the last coat of wax into the oak, and the workshop filled with the smell of lavender. The desk glowed like honey under the lamp, and every scar and ink stain on it looked like a line in a story.

One evening, as she was cleaning her brushes, the door opened, and Jonah stood there, out of breath, with rain in his hair. He carried a small walnut clock wrapped in a blue cloth, and he looked as if he had run from the station.

Jonah hung the little clock on the wall above her workbench, set the hands carefully and wound the tiny key. It began to tick softly and steadily, and the old workshop sounded different at once, as if it had been waiting for a heartbeat.
He said that it had been silent for forty years, and that he had mended its cracked case the way she had taught him. “It is for you,” he said, going red, “and I hope you do not mind the noise.”
Then he asked, in a rush, whether she would have dinner with him now, tonight, if she was not too tired. Iris looked at her stained overalls, laughed and went to wash her face and find a clean shirt.

The restaurant on the corner was small and warm, with candles in bottles on every table and steam on the windows. They were given the table in the back, and Jonah studied the menu as though it were a very difficult watch.

Over bread and olives, he told her that he had never eaten in a city restaurant, and that he was more nervous than he looked. Then he took a crumpled envelope from his jacket and slid it across the table without saying a word.

It was a letter, written in his small, careful hand and carried in his pocket for three weeks. It said that he had written it five times and almost never sent it, and that she made him braver than he had ever been.
Iris read it twice, with her hand over her mouth, while Jonah stared at the tablecloth. Then she pushed back her chair, walked round the table and kissed him, in front of the whole restaurant.

For a moment the room was silent, and then somebody at the next table began to clap, and then everybody did. A waiter appeared with a pudding, two spoons and a single candle, and said that it was with the compliments of the house.

It was raining when they came out, and they shared one umbrella, which was far too small for two. They walked slowly through the wet streets, their shoulders touching, and Jonah asked whether she would take the desk to Ruth on Saturday.
At the workshop door she stopped, with the key in her hand and rain running down her neck. “I am so glad you came,” she said, “and I shall say so as often as I can.”

On Saturday morning, Iris, Pia and Jonah wrapped the desk in thick blankets and carried it down the stairs, one step at a time. Nobody spoke except to say left and a bit more, and the desk slid into the borrowed van without a scratch.

They drove for two hours along the coast road, with the desk strapped down behind them and Pia talking happily in the back. Every time the van went round a corner, Iris looked in the mirror to make sure that the blankets had not moved.

Daniel was waiting at the gate of Harbour View in his best jacket, with a bunch of yellow daffodils in one hand. He had come on the train, he said, because he had not slept, and he had been standing there since nine.

Four of them carried the desk down the long corridor, past curious faces, into a sunny room at the end. A nurse had already cleared the corner beneath the window, and they set the desk there with great ceremony.

Ruth sat down in front of it and touched the pale ring of ink, as if it might still be wet. Then she found the two small letters under the drawer, and tears ran down her cheeks, although she was smiling.
Ruth slid out the secret drawer with one finger, smooth and silent, and looked into the empty space behind it. “How wonderful,” she said, “to see it with nothing hidden in it at all.”
Daniel took a paper bag from his pocket and laid out cream paper, envelopes and a book of stamps. Every one of the stamps, he said, was for a letter that would really be posted.

Ruth sat at the desk and wrote Dear Daniel at the top of a clean page, while Daniel, in the armchair, wrote Dear Ruth. They wrote for ten whole minutes, side by side and in perfect silence, and neither of them looked at the other's page.

Then, arm in arm, they walked down to the red post box at the end of the path, with Iris and Pia close behind. Ruth dropped her letter in first, Daniel dropped his in after it, and they listened to both fall with the same small, soft sound.

Ruth waved from her window as the van drove away, the old blue ribbon looped around her fingers. Daniel stood beside her, already arguing happily about whose letter would arrive first, and the afternoon light made them both look very young.

In April, Ruth told the staff at Harbour View that she wished to live in Saltmere again, if somebody would help her. The doctor frowned, the matron sighed, and then they both agreed, because nobody had ever seen her so determined.

Jonah found a small whitewashed cottage a few minutes from the lighthouse, with a blue door and a south-facing window. Its owner, who was Mrs Dunmore's cousin, said that she would be glad to let it to somebody who loved the sea.
Ruth packed for a week, deciding with great care which books to keep and which to give to the home's library. She put her glasses, her cardigans and the old biscuit tin into the same small suitcase.
Moving day came in late May, on a morning so clear that the sea looked painted. Jonah drove the blue van, with the desk roped in the back and Ruth beside him, holding her hat on against the wind.

After lunch, Ruth insisted on walking the harbour wall to the lighthouse, with her stick in one hand and Daniel's arm in the other. It took them half an hour, and they stopped three times to look at the sea, and she did not complain once.

That evening the desk stood under the cottage window, and Ruth sat down at it as if she had never been away. She wrote the date at the top of a clean page and began a letter to Daniel, who lived only three streets away.

On Monday she pushed open the door of Marsh and Son, and the little brass bell rang over her head. She stood very still among the ticking clocks, and then she walked to the counter and laid her hand flat on the worn wood.

A few days later, Ruth gave Iris tea in the cottage and told her about her life. She had been a librarian for forty years, and she had loved nearly all of them, because a library is a place where nobody hurries.
Her life had been quiet but not unhappy, she said, with good friends and good books. She had only one real regret, and she put her old fountain pen into Iris's hand as if it explained everything.
“Do not keep your words in a drawer,” said Ruth, closing Iris's fingers around the pen. “A word is worth nothing until it reaches someone, and I learned that rather late.”
In June, a letter from her landlord told Iris that the lease on her workshop would end in September. She read it three times, and then she realised that she was not at all sorry.
She told Pia over the phone, and Pia said at once that she should go to Saltmere. “You are never so happy as when you talk about that town,” she said, “and I shall visit every month.”
On her next visit, Iris noticed a To Let sign in an empty shop on Quay Street, two doors from Marsh and Son. The glass was dusty, but the window was tall and wide, and it faced north.

The landlord, Mr Pascoe, was a small man with large keys, and he unlocked the door with a flourish. Inside, dust floated in the sunlight, and there was a high ceiling, a stone floor and a sink in the back room.

Iris stood in the middle of the floor and turned slowly round, seeing benches and clamps and half-mended chairs. The north light was soft and even, and she told Mr Pascoe, with only a little wobble, that she would take it.

That evening she told Jonah, and he lifted her off the floor and spun her round until the clocks began to chime. When he put her down, they were both laughing, and a very old clock on the top shelf struck thirteen.

Jonah painted the sign himself in the evenings, with gold letters on a dark green board that read Calloway, Furniture Restorer. Daniel supervised from a chair, and said that the C was a little too enthusiastic, which Jonah said was how he liked it.

In August, the village hall held its summer dance, as it had for a hundred years, with paper lanterns strung from beam to beam. The whole town went, and Ruth wore a new blue dress and, in her white hair, the old blue ribbon.

When the band played the same slow waltz, Daniel stood up, offered Ruth his arm and led her onto the floor. They danced very slowly, with her stick hooked over a chair, and when the music stopped, the whole hall applauded.
Then Jonah asked Iris to dance, and within three steps he trod firmly on her foot. “Now I understand,” said Iris, laughing so hard she had to hold his sleeve, “why this story is told in your family.”

On a warm evening in late summer, the four of them sat on the harbour wall with their legs over the water. The sun went down behind the lighthouse, and Iris thought that there was nowhere else in the world that she wanted to be.

Ruth took a letter from her handbag and read it aloud, a short, funny note from Daniel that the postman had delivered that morning. Daniel pretended to be embarrassed, but he was smiling so widely that the gulls came closer to see what was wrong.

Iris said, as lightly as she could, that she must go back to the city one last time, to pack the workshop. Jonah offered to come with her, but she shook her head, because this was something that she wanted to finish by herself.

In the city, Pia arrived on Thursday in her oldest jeans, with rolls of tape and a flask of coffee. Together they wrapped the clamps and chisels, and when they found their mother's wooden plane, Pia said it belonged in the new shop.

By Friday night, the van was packed to the roof, and the workshop was swept and empty and strangely large. Pia hugged her, promised to see her in Saltmere on Sunday and drove away, and Iris was left alone with the ticking clock.

She sat down at the bare bench, where she had spent so many nights, and took Ruth's black fountain pen from her pocket. In front of her lay one clean sheet of paper, and for a long time she did nothing but look at it.

Then she began to write, slowly at first and then faster, the words that she would never have dared to say aloud. She wrote that she was afraid, that she was happier than she had ever been, and that she loved him.

She read it through once, folded it in three and sealed it in an envelope. On the front she wrote Jonah Marsh, Marsh and Son, Quay Street, Saltmere, and she pressed a first-class stamp on the corner with her thumb.
The street was dark and quiet, and the lamps made little yellow pools on the pavement. Iris walked to the red post box on the corner with the letter held tightly, as Ruth must once have walked.

She held it above the slot for a long moment, and then she let it go and heard it fall. The letter would arrive a day after she did, which was perfectly foolish, but some words are worth nothing until they are sent.

Her father, a banker with a gift for disapproval, was waiting for a new post in the city and had rented a tall grey house above the harbour for the rest of the summer. Ruth was nineteen, clever and restless, and she wrote that Saltmere had looked to her at first like the end of the world.

Her father had rules for everything, from the hour at which she rose to the novels she might read, and he kept them with the quiet thoroughness of a man who balanced other people's accounts for a living. For two long weeks Ruth walked the harbour alone, bored and a little angry, with nobody to talk to but the gulls and her mother's gentle sighs. She wrote that she had begun to believe that nothing in Saltmere would ever happen, and that this was the one thing she had been wrong about.

Then, in the middle of August, her wristwatch stopped without warning, and she wandered into the narrow streets behind the harbour in search of someone who could mend it. On Quay Street she found a shop whose window was crowded with clocks of every size, all ticking at slightly different speeds, like a roomful of people talking at once. The sign above the door read Marsh and Son, and a little brass bell announced her with such enthusiasm that she almost turned and ran.

Behind the counter, a young man with a magnifying glass screwed into one eye looked up, took her watch without a word and opened it with tools no bigger than eyelashes. Within minutes he had found a speck of grit in the works, blown it away and set the little hands ticking again, and he did it all so gently that Ruth forgot to be shy. When she reached for her purse he shook his head, and then, going red to his ears, he asked whether she would care to come to the dance at the village hall on Saturday.

On Saturday evening Ruth told her parents that she had a headache and retired to her room with great dignity, and then she slipped down the back stairs and out through the kitchen door. She had tied her hair with the only ribbon she possessed that was not sensible, a blue one, bought in secret with her own pocket money, and she felt wonderfully reckless as she hurried down the hill. By the time she reached the village hall, her heart was pounding so hard that she was afraid the whole street could hear it.

Inside, paper lanterns in yellow, green and rose were strung from beam to beam, and a small band of fiddle, accordion and drum was working its way through a slow waltz. Daniel was waiting by the door in a jacket that was a little too short in the sleeves, and when he held out his hand, Ruth took it before she could change her mind. She had never danced with a boy in her life, and within three steps she had trodden firmly on his foot.

Daniel did not wince; he only laughed and said that his foot had survived worse, and that it was an honour to be trodden on by someone so clearly in earnest. Ruth laughed too, helplessly, and the laughter loosened something in her chest that had been tight since the day her family left home. They danced and talked until the band packed away its instruments, and she told him things that she had never said aloud to anyone.

When the lanterns were finally put out, Daniel offered to walk her home, and he took her the long way, out along the harbour wall, with the sea breathing quietly on either side. At the far end the white lighthouse stood against the stars, and he told her, with the shy pride of a boy describing a friend, that its lamp had never once failed in his father's memory. Ruth wrote that she had looked up at that steady light and thought, quite clearly, that she would like to be a person who never failed anybody either.

Iris put the page down and discovered that she was smiling, which was ridiculous, because it was nearly two in the morning and the girl in the letter must be an old woman now, if she was still alive. She got up, put the kettle on again and stood at the window with her arms folded, trying to remember the last time she had been so curious about anything that was not made of wood. Somewhere in a town she had never visited, she thought, a lighthouse had been shining all that time, and the thought gave her an odd, tender ache beneath the ribs.

That first night, Ruth wrote, she lay awake in the attic bedroom with the window open and listened to the sea, and she could still hear the waltz playing somewhere inside her head. Her foot, she noticed, was still tapping beneath the blanket, and her face ached from smiling in the dark. She had come to Saltmere believing that nothing would happen, and she fell asleep at last, near dawn, with the strange and frightening feeling that everything had.

Daniel led her up a narrow staircase to the workshop above the shop, where perhaps thirty clocks ticked on every wall and shelf in a gentle, disagreeing chorus. His father, old Walter Marsh, sat at a bench by the window with a lens in his eye and a watch in pieces before him, and he looked up only to nod to her with grave courtesy. Ruth had expected to be an intruder, but she wrote that she had never felt so quietly welcome anywhere in her life.

Over the following days Daniel taught her how a clock works: how the spring pulls, how the wheels turn, and how a tiny lever lets the time out one tick at a time. Ruth wound a heavy brass clock under his guidance, and his hands, steady from years of delicate work, closed over hers to show her how gently it must be done. A clock, he told her, is only patience made into a machine, and she wrote that she had gone home that night and looked at her own ticking heart with new respect.

One bright morning they borrowed a small blue rowing boat from a fisherman who owed Daniel's father a favour, and they pulled out beyond the harbour wall towards the rocks beneath the lighthouse. Daniel let Ruth take the oars, and she laughed so much at her own splashing that for ten minutes they travelled in a magnificent circle. Beyond the harbour the sea was green and clear, and looking back, she saw the whole of Saltmere spread out like a toy town, with a single thread of smoke rising from the baker's chimney.

Nearly every day they ate their sandwiches on the harbour wall, watched with great interest by a row of gulls who regarded each crumb as a personal debt. Daniel said that he would be a clockmaker like his father and his grandfather before him, and that he could think of nothing better than mending other people's time. Ruth, by contrast, said that she knew only what she did not want, which was the sensible, tidy future her father had already arranged for her.

Each evening Ruth came home a little later, with salt drying in her hair and her shoes swinging from her fingers, and each evening she braced herself for the sound of her father's voice. It was her mother who met her in the hall, a tired, gentle woman who had given up arguing with her husband years ago, and who looked at her daughter's shining face and said nothing at all. She only smiled, very slightly, and turned down the lamp, and Ruth wrote that she had loved her mother more in that silence than in all the words she had ever heard.

One wet afternoon they sat together in the quiet shop while rain ran down the window and the clocks ticked around them like a slow and affectionate crowd. Daniel read her a poem he had copied out in his best handwriting, stumbling a little over the long words, and she listened as though nobody had ever read to her before. When he had finished, she told him the secret she had told no one, that she longed to go to university and live among books, and he said he had never doubted it.

At the beginning of September her father came home with a telegram in his hand and a look of cold triumph on his face. His new post in the city was ready, he announced, and the whole family would leave on the seventh. Then, in a voice like a closing door, he added that he had heard certain things in the town and that she would not be speaking to the clockmaker's boy again.

Ruth did not obey, of course, and on the last evening she ran along the harbour wall to the foot of the lighthouse, where Daniel was waiting with his collar turned up against the wind. She told him everything in a rush, the telegram, the seventh, her father's voice, and he listened with his head bowed, saying nothing, until she had finished. Then he took both her hands in his, and in the slow sweep of the lamplight he promised that he would write to her every week.

Then Daniel made her promise one more thing, that she would find a way to come back for a single day, on the eleven o'clock train on Saturday the seventh of October. Ruth wrote her new address on the back of a ticket, and he folded it into his waistcoat pocket as carefully as if it were the mainspring of the world. He swore that he would be standing on the platform in his best jacket, and she swore that nothing on earth would keep her away.

On the seventh of September the car stood packed outside the grey house, and Ruth's father counted the suitcases twice, as though he suspected one of having plans of its own. She sat in the back seat with her hands in her lap and her ribbon in her pocket, and she did not cry until the road turned and the white lighthouse shrank to a pin. Her mother's hand found hers on the seat, and neither of them said a word all the way to the city.

The Ashbys' new home was a tall, grey house in the city, with iron railings, a dark front hall and a brass plate on the door that announced her father's importance to the neighbours. Within a week he had arranged her days from morning to night, beginning with a course in typing and bookkeeping that he considered a sensible foundation for a young woman of good family. Ruth sat at the back of the class with her hands on the keys, thinking of clocks, and the machines clattered like a hundred small, disapproving voices.

After three weeks of silence Ruth gathered all her courage and asked her father, as politely as she knew how, whether she might make one short visit to Saltmere before the winter. He did not even lower his newspaper; he merely turned a page and remarked that the clockmaker's boy would have forgotten her by Christmas and that there was nothing in that town for a girl of her prospects. She stood in the doorway for a moment longer, waiting for someone, anyone, to say that he was wrong, and then she went upstairs and closed her door very quietly.

On the seventh of October her father sent her and her mother to take tea with a distant cousin on the far side of the city, and he refused to hear a word of protest. Ruth sat bolt upright on a horsehair sofa in a stranger's drawing room, balancing a cup that rattled in its saucer, and tried to answer questions about the weather. When the clock on the mantelpiece struck eleven, she shut her eyes and saw Daniel on the platform in his best jacket, searching every window of the train.

On Monday night, when the house was quiet, Ruth sat at the small oak desk that her father had bought her for her studies and began, at last, to write. She poured onto the page everything that she had swallowed for a month, the anger and the longing and the shame of a girl who had not been brave enough to simply get on a train. When the ink had dried, she read it over once and knew, with a cold and certain feeling, that she would never be able to post it.

She opened the right-hand drawer to hide the letter, but the drawer stuck halfway, and in her impatience she tugged it right out of the desk. Behind it, in the dark, there was a hollow space that no one could have guessed at, exactly deep enough for a bundle of folded paper. Ruth knelt on the carpet looking into it, and she had the odd, comforting feeling that the desk had been waiting all along to be trusted with a secret.

On Wednesday she copied Daniel's address onto an envelope in her best handwriting, put on her hat and coat, and walked the whole mile to the post office without stopping once. She stood in the queue for ten minutes, with the envelope held against her chest like a shield, and rehearsed what she would say to the clerk. When she reached the counter her voice failed her entirely, and she turned around and walked home through the drizzle without having bought so much as a stamp.

Every morning she waited in the hall for the postman, pretending to tie a shoe or straighten a picture, and every morning the letters on the mat were addressed to her father. By the middle of November she had stopped hoping, and on a foggy night she wrote a second letter, in which she asked Daniel whether he was well and whether the lighthouse lamp still shone. She did not ask the one question that mattered, and she folded the page small and slid it behind the drawer beside the first.

Her father invited a young banker named Mr Whitlock to dinner, and Ruth saw at once, from the way her mother's hands trembled over the soup, exactly what was being arranged. Mr Whitlock was tall, well-dressed and perfectly pleasant, and he spoke at length about interest rates while she nodded in the right places. When he asked at last what she liked to read, she lifted her eyes from her plate and said, very distinctly, that she preferred letters.

At Christmas snow lay thick on the pillar box at the end of the road, and Ruth stood in front of it in the early dark with a card in her gloved hand. She held it over the slot for so long that her fingers went numb, and she could hear her own heart, and the faint sound of carols from a window across the street. In the end she put the card back in her pocket and walked home with her head down, and the snow filled her footprints behind her as though she had never been there.

On New Year's Eve, while the church bells rang out across the city and her parents toasted a prosperous future in the drawing room, Ruth sat alone at the oak desk and gathered the few letters she had written. She tied them together with the blue ribbon she had worn to the dance, tightening the bow with a care that was almost a prayer. She promised herself that she would post them all in the spring, and she slid them behind the drawer, and the drawer closed with a soft, obedient sound.

In the spring of 1962, Ruth finished her course and, to her father's great annoyance, took a post as an assistant at a small public library, where the shelves smelled of dust and paste and possibility. She wrote that she was happier among the rows of spines than she had been all winter, and that she felt, for the first time since September, that her days belonged to her. Every month she wrote Daniel another letter, and every month it joined the others behind the drawer, where the bundle slowly grew.

One night in the kitchen, when the house was asleep and the kettle had gone cold, Ruth's mother finally told her the truth, with tears running openly down her face. Four letters had come from Saltmere that autumn, in a boyish hand that she had recognised at once, and her husband had written Return to Sender across every one and put them back in the post unopened. She had said nothing then out of fear, she whispered, and she had said nothing since out of shame, and she begged her daughter to forgive a woman who had been a coward for twenty years of marriage.

Ruth ran upstairs, then down again, and finally stood outside her father's study with her hand raised to knock and her whole body shaking with a fury she had never known. Through the door she could hear the dry, steady scratch of his pen, the sound of a man who had never once doubted that he was right. She stood there until the clock in the hall struck midnight, and then she went back to bed without having made a sound, and she hated herself more than she hated him.

In her next letter she wrote that Daniel must have believed she had sent his letters back herself, and that the thought was unbearable. Instead of setting her free, the truth only made the task heavier, because every month that passed turned a simple letter into a confession, and she could no longer imagine the first sentence. She had waited too long, she wrote, and the waiting had grown a wall around her, brick by brick, until she could no longer see over it.

In the winter of 1963 a friend of her mother's wrote from Saltmere with the town's news, and in the middle of a paragraph about a lost fishing boat and a new vicar, one sentence caught in Ruth's throat. The clockmaker's son, it said, was walking out with a kind girl named Margaret, and the whole of Saltmere expected a wedding before the summer. Ruth read it at her desk in the library, set down her pile of returned books with extreme care, and sat looking at the wall for a very long time.

In the spring of 1963 Ruth wrote her last letter to Daniel, and it was the shortest and the plainest of them all. She said that she was glad he was happy, that she wished the lighthouse lamp a hundred more years, and that she had never posted a single letter, because she had been too frightened. She ended with a line so simple that she was surprised her hand did not shake as she wrote it, and then she tied the page into the bundle and closed the drawer for the last time.

Iris read the last letter twice, and the second time her hands began to shake, because the thin paper was spotted with the faint rings of old tears. The writer had tried to dry them, and the ink had blurred in places, so that certain words seemed to be disappearing even as Iris looked at them. Its final line was so plain and so brave that she had to put one hand over her mouth, and she did not dare to read it a third time.

By now the sky beyond the workshop window was turning from black to grey, and somewhere in the yard the first bird was trying out a few uncertain notes. Iris sat on the floor among the sawdust with the letters in her lap, and for a long while she did not move at all. It was a quiet, uncomfortable thought: for all her cleverness with wood and wax, she was no better than Ruth at saying what she felt.

At last she took her phone from her pocket and opened a folder that she had never shown to a living soul, a folder she had named, with a small and bitter joke, Drafts. It held dozens of messages written late at night in careful, honest words, and not one of them had ever been sent. She scrolled through them slowly in the grey light, and it felt like walking through a house where every room had been prepared for guests who never came.

There were messages to old friends, to a landlord who had once been kind to her, and to a teacher she had admired and never thanked. The oldest of all, from two years ago, began, “Pia, I am sorry about the house,” and ended with three lines that Iris could not bring herself to read again. It had sat there ever since, unsent, a small and silent stone that she carried everywhere she went.

By the time the sun had properly risen, Iris had read every draft in the folder, and she saw them for the first time as a single body of work. They were kind, brave and honest, and each had been abandoned at the very last moment, as though some sensible hand had reached out and stopped her at the edge of a pavement. She made strong coffee, drank it standing, and felt in her chest the slow discomfort of recognising someone whom she had never expected to meet.

Two years earlier, after their mother's funeral, Iris and her sister Pia had stood in the narrow hall of the house on Pell Road, surrounded by half-packed boxes and the smell of a life that had stopped. They had promised each other that they would sort everything gently, over one quiet weekend, and the promise had lasted until the first cupboard. By Sunday evening they were no longer speaking, and the house, which had held a family for thirty years, held only silence.

Pia, who was worried about money, wanted to sell the house at once, and she said so in a voice that Iris had heard as brisk and cold. Iris wanted to keep it exactly as it was, with the kettle on the hob and the tools in the shed, and she said so in a voice that Pia had heard as stubborn and childish. Each of them had thrown a sentence that could not be caught, and each had left that house believing that it was the other who ought to telephone.

Their mother had been a carpenter's daughter with a gift for patient work, and it was she who had put the first sheet of sandpaper into Iris's small hands and taught her to follow the grain. Her wooden plane still sat on the workbench, its handle worn smooth by decades of use, and some evenings Iris picked it up merely to feel its familiar weight. She had never told anyone that she spoke to it sometimes, quietly, when the workshop was empty, and that it had never once interrupted.

She began a fresh message to Pia, deleted the first line, wrote it again in different words and deleted it a second time, until the little cursor blinked at her like a patient, reproachful eye. Her own tiredness defeated her in the end, for she had not slept at all, and she lay down on the old sofa in the corner of the workshop with the phone face down on her chest. She slept for three hours, deeply and without dreams, and when she woke, the sun had moved across the whole floor.

At noon she woke with a stiff neck and a single clear purpose, and she carried her laptop to the bench and typed the word Saltmere into the search bar. The town appeared at once, in a handful of photographs: a grey harbour, a row of painted fishing boats, and a white lighthouse standing at the end of a long stone wall. A little further down the page, in a plain blue link that looked as though it had been made years ago and never touched, was a shop called Marsh and Son, clockmakers, Quay Street.

There was a telephone number at the bottom of the page, and Iris dialled it before she could lose her nerve, pacing the length of the workshop with the phone pressed to her ear. It rang and rang in what she imagined to be a narrow room full of ticking clocks, with a brass bell above the door and nobody coming to answer. After the fifteenth ring she hung up, and she sat very still for a moment, feeling rather as though she had knocked on a door in a dream.

She could simply post the letters, she thought, with a note and a stamp, and let the post office finish a journey that had never begun. But a parcel of old words arriving on a doormat seemed too small and too cold for what they were, and it might be opened by anyone, or by no one at all. These letters had waited long enough, and they deserved to be put into the right hands by somebody who knew what they had cost.

She remembered that Mr Fenn had pressed a card into her hand at the auction, and she found it in the pocket of her work apron, creased and dusty, with a telephone number in faded blue ink. When he answered, she tried to explain, in a rush that made no sense even to herself, that she had found something behind a drawer of the desk and needed to know whose it had been. There was a long pause on the line, and then the old man said, in a voice suddenly warm with curiosity, that he would be very glad to help.

Mr Fenn did not need long to look it up, and he told her that the desk had come from the flat of a Miss Ruth Ashby, whose niece had cleared it the previous winter in a hurry. He did not know whether Miss Ashby was living or dead, he admitted, but he promised to telephone the niece that same afternoon and ask. Iris wrote the name on her notepad in large capital letters, Ruth Ashby, and looked at it as though it might get up and speak.

That evening Mr Fenn telephoned to say, with many apologies, that Ruth Ashby's niece was away until Monday and could not be reached, and that he would go on trying. Iris thanked him, put down the phone and looked for a long while at the bundle of letters lying on the bench beside the cold teapot. She had spent two years waiting for someone else to move first, she realised, and she decided, all at once and without any fuss, that she would take the letters to Saltmere herself.

She was at the station before six the next morning, with a small bag, a flask of tea and the letters wrapped in her good scarf at the very bottom, like something that might break. The first train of the day was cold and almost empty, and as it pulled out, the city fell away behind the window in a long grey blur of roofs and cranes. Iris pressed her forehead against the glass, and for the first time in two years she felt that she was travelling towards something rather than away from it.

Opposite her sat an old woman in a green coat, knitting something long and shapeless from a ball of matching wool, who looked up and asked, in the friendliest way, where she was going. When Iris told her, she laughed with great kindness and explained that nobody went to Saltmere in March, except for love or for funerals. She added that her own husband had proposed to her on the harbour wall there in 1958, in a gale, and that she had not heard a word he said and had said yes regardless.

Iris admitted that her errand was a little of both, and the old woman nodded, as though it were the most sensible answer she had ever heard.
