She went back to her knitting, counting stitches under her breath, and then said, without looking up, that one of the great mistakes of her life had been waiting for the right words. They never come, she said, and in the end you must simply open your mouth and let the wrong ones out.

About two hours into the journey the land seemed to give way, and the sea appeared on the left, wide and grey and shining beneath a lid of low cloud. The railway ran along the edge of the cliffs, so close that Iris could see the white lines of surf drawing themselves on the sand far below. Then, far along the coast, small and clean and white against the sky, she caught sight of a lighthouse, and her heart gave a strange, unreasonable jump of recognition.

The train deposited her at a tiny station with a single platform, a wooden bench and a clock whose hands had stopped at ten past four, perhaps years ago. Nobody else got off, and the guard waved a flag at nothing in particular and the train slid away, leaving her alone with the wind. Iris stood on the cold boards and thought of a young man in his best jacket who had once waited exactly there, searching every window of a train that did not carry what he was hoping for.

She followed a steep lane down the hill between slate roofs and crooked chimneys, and with every step the smell of salt and seaweed grew stronger, until it seemed to fill her whole head. Washing flapped in tiny gardens, a bicycle leaned against a blue door, and a ginger cat observed her from a wall with the air of someone who had been told to expect her. Somewhere below, a boat engine coughed twice and caught, and the gulls rose up in a cloud, complaining.

At the bottom of the hill lay the harbour, where fishing boats rocked at their moorings and nets lay heaped on the quay like sleeping animals. Gulls wheeled and quarrelled overhead, and a man in yellow oilskins looked up from a lobster pot to give her a slow, appraising nod. At the end of the longer wall, far out, stood the lighthouse, tall and white and exactly as the letters had described it.

Quay Street ran along the edge of the water, a row of narrow, weather-beaten houses with a baker, a chandler and a shop that sold nothing but string. Halfway down she found it, a tall and shabby front painted a faded green, with the words Marsh and Son in gold letters that had mostly flaked away. The window was crowded with clocks of every size, ticking out of time with one another, and Iris stood in front of it for a full minute, trying to feel brave.

At last she pushed open the door, and a little brass bell rang over her head with such enthusiasm that she almost laughed, because it was exactly the bell that had greeted Ruth sixty-five years before. The shop was long and narrow and warm, and it smelled of oil and brass and old wood, and it was filled from floor to ceiling with the soft, overlapping sound of ticking. Behind the counter a tall young man looked up from the watch he was mending, a lens screwed into one eye, and he did not smile.

The young man lifted the lens from his eye and asked, a little stiffly and without much hope of an interesting answer, whether he could help her. Iris had practised a graceful speech all the way from the city, and it vanished completely, so that all she could say was that she was looking for Daniel Marsh. The words sounded absurd in the warm, ticking quiet, like a question asked aloud in a church by someone who had wandered in by mistake.

He did not answer at once, and she could see him weighing her up, the way a man might weigh an unfamiliar coin. People had come to this shop before, he said at last, with clipboards and charming smiles, and some of them had called on his grandfather when he was alone, and not all of them had been honest. He hoped she would forgive him, therefore, for asking who she was and what exactly she wanted from an old man who had nothing worth stealing.

Iris did not know where to begin, so she did the simplest thing she could think of, unwrapping her scarf and laying the bundle of old letters on the glass counter between them. The blue ribbon, which had come loose on the train, slid away, and the envelopes fanned out across the counter like fallen leaves. Every one of them, she saw with fresh eyes, carried the same name and the same faded address, the name of the shop in which they now lay.

The young man bent over the nearest envelope and read the address, and Iris explained that every letter had been written by a woman named Ruth Ashby. He was Jonah Marsh, he said, Daniel Marsh's grandson, and he had never in his life heard of any Ruth Ashby. He touched the paper with one careful finger, as though it might crumble, and asked how on earth a letter to this shop could have lain unposted for sixty years.

So Iris told him everything, from the auction to the stuck drawer and the hidden space behind it, and she told it badly, because her hands would not stop trembling. She told him about the girl who wrote to a boy and never posted a line, and about the waltz, the lanterns and the lighthouse lamp that had never failed. As she spoke, the suspicion drained slowly from his face, and what replaced it was something more careful, and more tender, and a good deal more frightened.

When she had finished, Jonah said nothing for a long moment, and then he crossed the shop, turned the sign on the door to Closed and filled a dented kettle at the little sink in the corner. Marsh and Son had stood on that corner for more than a hundred years, he remarked, over his shoulder, and it had never once closed in the middle of a working day. Iris understood that this was his way of saying that something extraordinary had happened, and that he did not yet have any other words for it.

Over tea in two chipped mugs, Jonah explained that Daniel was his grandfather, that he had taught him the trade in the workshop upstairs, and that his grandmother Margaret had died six years ago after a long illness. He nodded towards a photograph beside the till, in which a small, round, laughing woman held up a trout as though it were a trophy. Since then, he said, his grandfather had grown quiet, and spent most of his days on the harbour wall, feeding the gulls and watching the lighthouse.

Jonah said that his grandfather hardly ever spoke of the old days, but that once, when he was about ten, he had told him about a girl who trod on his foot at a dance. He had laughed so much, his grandfather said, that he forgot the pain, and he had never found another partner to match her for sheer enthusiasm. Iris felt the hair rise on her arms, because she knew that story already, and had read it the night before by lamplight.

Jonah locked the shop, tied the letters back into her scarf with great care, and walked beside her along the harbour, with his hands deep in his pockets and his shoulders hunched against the wind. He was a quiet man, with the careful, patient look of someone who spent his days among small and delicate things, and he talked mostly about clocks. Iris suspected, listening, that the ticking made his silences easier to bear, and she found, rather to her surprise, that she did not mind them at all.

The wind rose as they neared the end of the long stone wall, and there, at the very tip, stood an old man in a patched coat, with a paper bag in his hand. He was throwing crusts one at a time to a crowd of gulls, with the grave attention of a conductor, and the birds were quarrelling beautifully over each one. Jonah stopped walking and said, very quietly, that this was his grandfather, and Iris saw that he was suddenly afraid this might not be a kindness.

Jonah called out across the wind, and the old man turned slowly, one hand lifted against the glare, his white hair blowing in untidy wisps about his forehead. He was thin and a little bent, with the pale look of a man who had spent his life indoors, but his eyes were bright and kind. He looked at his grandson with such open and uncomplicated pleasure that Iris felt, absurdly, as though she were about to break something precious.

Daniel shook Iris's hand with old-fashioned courtesy, holding it a moment longer than strangers do, and then he turned to his grandson with raised eyebrows. Closing the shop on a working day, he observed, was a thing he had never lived to see, and he hoped that nobody had died. Company on the end of the wall was rare, he added, with a gentle smile, and the gulls would be quite jealous.

Iris took a deep breath, because there was no gentle way to begin, and said that she thought he had once known a girl called Ruth Ashby. The crust of bread slid out of Daniel's fingers and fell between the stones, and the gulls swooped on it with a scream that neither of them noticed. He lowered himself onto the wall very slowly, like a man whose legs had suddenly remembered how old they were.

For a long time he said nothing at all, and the sea went on slapping against the wall below, and the gulls wheeled and complained above his head. His hands lay open on his knees, and Iris saw that they were shaking, the fine, quick shaking of hands that had once been steady enough to repair a watch. When at last he asked how she knew that name, she sat down beside him on the cold stone and explained, as gently as she could, about the desk, the drawer and the letters.

Jonah led them to a wooden bench in the shelter of the lighthouse wall, where the wind could not reach, and Daniel sat with his hands on his knees and his eyes on the horizon. In sixty-five years, he said, he had told the story of that summer to one person only, and that person had been Margaret, who had listened without a flicker of jealousy. He had never told his grandson the whole of it, and he thought that the moment had come.

He had met a girl at a dance in the summer of 1961, he said, and for three weeks he had been happier than he had known a person could be. On the seventh of October, in his best jacket, with his hair combed flat with water, he stood on the platform at Saltmere and waited for the eleven o'clock train. She was not on that one, nor on the next, nor on the last train of the evening, and he walked home in the dark carrying a bunch of flowers that had begun to droop.

Four times that autumn he wrote to the address on the ticket, and four times the envelope came back unopened, with Return to Sender scrawled across it in a hand he did not know. He kept them in a biscuit tin and never had the heart to open them, and in the end he decided that she had thought better of him and had been too kind to say so. He did not write a fifth, and he never blamed her, but for the rest of his life he could not pass the station without glancing at the clock.

Without a word Iris untied her scarf, found the first letter, the one dated the ninth of October, 1961, and laid it in his open hands as though it were a bird. Daniel put on his reading glasses, which took him three attempts, and then he began to read aloud in a low, unsteady voice that grew a little firmer with every line. It was a long letter, and he read it slowly, with a pause after each sentence, as if it were a thing that had to be handled with great care and might still be spoiled.

When he reached the passage in which Ruth described the clock in a stranger's drawing room striking eleven, his voice cracked like thin ice and then stopped altogether. He took off his glasses and wept, quite openly and without shame, the tears running into the deep lines of his face, and the sea went on breathing against the wall as though it had heard such things before. Jonah put an arm around his shoulders, as gently as he would have lifted a watch from its case, and Daniel leaned his white head against his grandson's shoulder and let himself be held.

When he could speak again, Daniel wiped his face with the back of his hand, took both of Iris's hands in his own, and asked, very quietly, whether Ruth was alive. Iris said that she did not know, because the man at the auction house had not yet been able to find out, but that she would not rest until she did. The sun was going down over the sea in long bars of gold and rose, and she made the promise with the lighthouse standing over them like a witness.

The last train had gone, Jonah pointed out, and the next would not leave until morning, and he would not hear of her sleeping on the platform. He walked her up the hill to a guesthouse with a blue door, where Mrs Dunmore, a large and cheerful woman in a flowered apron, looked Iris up and down and declared that she was far too thin. Within ten minutes Iris had been given a bowl of soup, a hot-water bottle and a narrow room under the roof whose window was entirely filled with the sea.

At dusk Jonah appeared at the guesthouse door with two parcels of fish and chips, wrapped in paper that had already gone transparent with grease and glory, and suggested that the best table in Saltmere was the harbour wall. They sat side by side with their legs dangling over the water and ate with their fingers, while a row of gulls lined up along the stones to observe them with undisguised greed. A particularly bold one snatched a chip from Iris's hand, and for the first time that day Jonah threw back his head and laughed out loud.

Between mouthfuls he told her that he had learned his trade at his grandfather's elbow, that he had once dreamed of leaving Saltmere to study engineering in a city, and that he had somehow never got round to going. Iris said that she had learned hers from her mother, who had taught her to read the grain of a plank the way other people read a face. They discovered, as the light went, that they shared a quiet dislike of hurry and a great liking for things that had been made with care.

As the last daylight drained from the sky, a bright spark appeared at the top of the lighthouse, and then a slow white beam began to sweep across the dark water, touching the boats and the wall in turn. Jonah said that his grandfather had taught him to love that lamp before he could read, because it had never once failed in his grandfather's memory, not even on the night of the great storm. Iris, watching the beam come round again, thought of a girl of nineteen looking up at that same steady light, and she felt the sixty-five years between them fold up like a letter.

Back in her little room under the roof, Iris lay awake with the window open, listening to the waves breaking against the harbour wall and the distant, patient clang of a buoy. She tried to compose a message to Pia, but every opening line was either too proud or too humble, and her mind kept sliding sideways towards a quiet man with a deep laugh. At last she gave up, turned on her side and let the sea rock her towards sleep, and the phone lay dark on the pillow beside her, still unsent.

In the morning Jonah took her up the narrow stairs behind the shop to the workshop where his grandfather and his great-grandfather had worked before him, a long room of north light and sloping floors. Trays of tiny wheels, springs and screws lay under shaded lamps, and clocks stood in pieces on every bench, their innards laid out in tidy rows like the contents of a very small, very orderly city. Iris, who loved a good workshop as other people loved a good view, stood in the doorway for a moment and simply breathed.

Jonah picked up a spring finer than a hair with a pair of tweezers, held it to the window and explained that most of his work was waiting, because a clock cannot be hurried any more than a tide. Iris, who had just spent a whole winter waiting for a coat of shellac to cure, told him that her own trade was exactly the same. They stood together in the cold, bright room, two people who had both chosen slow things in a fast world, and she felt a small, unexpected glow of kinship.

On the end of the bench lay a walnut clock case with a long, ugly crack running down one side, which a customer had brought in the week before, and Jonah sighed when he saw her looking at it. Cases, he confessed, were not his gift, and he had been putting it off for days in the hope that it might mend itself. Iris looked at it for a moment with her head on one side, the way a doctor looks at a patient, and then she rolled up her sleeves and asked for glue, a clamp and a cloth.

She showed him how to work the glue deep into the crack with a thin blade, and how to bring the two edges together with a clamp, tightening it by the smallest turns. Jonah leaned in beside her to watch, so close that she could smell the oil and brass in his sleeve, and when they both reached for the clamp at the same moment, his hand closed over hers. Neither of them moved, and neither looked up, and the clocks ticked on all around them, as though they had seen this sort of thing before and were far too polite to comment.

While the glue dried, Iris found herself telling him, haltingly, about the folder on her phone, the dozens of messages that she had written in the small hours and never had the courage to send. She had expected him to smile politely or to change the subject, but Jonah put down his cloth and listened with his whole attention, and when she had finished he was quiet for a moment. Then he said, in a voice that was kind and perfectly steady, that she should send the one to her sister, and that he thought she already knew it.

That afternoon, while the glue was still drying on the walnut case, Iris's phone began to ring in her pocket, and the voice on the line was Mr Fenn's, breathless with importance. He had spoken to Ruth Ashby's niece at last, he told her, and the niece had been astonished to learn that the old desk had given up a secret after so many years. Ruth Ashby herself was alive, said Mr Fenn, eighty-four years old and as sharp as a tack, and Iris had to sit down on a workshop stool because her knees had abruptly stopped being reliable.

She was living, he said, in a care home called Harbour View, about two hours' drive along the coast, where she had moved in the autumn after a fall on the stairs of her flat. He read out the address twice, slowly, as if he were reading a sacred text, and the line crackled with his obvious delight. Iris had no paper within reach, so she took the black pen from Jonah's bench and wrote the address on the back of her own hand, in capital letters, and pressed down hard.

She and Jonah almost ran along the harbour and up a lane behind the fish market to Daniel's cottage, a low whitewashed house with a blue gate and a crooked chimney. They found him in the kitchen, peeling potatoes at the table with the slow concentration of a man who had long since stopped expecting visitors. When Iris told him, he laid down the knife and wiped his hands on a tea towel, one finger at a time, and then he sat perfectly still, as though any movement might break the news.

On the mantelpiece above the stove stood a photograph of Margaret in a straw summer hat, laughing at whoever held the camera, and Daniel's eyes went to it and stayed there. She had known all about Ruth, he said, from the first year of their marriage, because he had never been able to lie to her, and she had never once minded. Everyone ought to keep a window open in their heart, Margaret used to say, and it was only polite to let the occupant of that room come and go as she pleased.

He was afraid, he confessed, that Ruth would be a stranger now, and that he would be one to her, two old people with nothing left in common except a dance. Iris answered that strangers did not keep their letters tied with a blue ribbon behind a drawer for sixty years, and Daniel looked at her for a moment and then nodded slowly. He went upstairs without another word and came back down with a biscuit tin, dented and rusty, that held four sealed envelopes, and he held it against his chest as though it were a sleeping child.

The next morning Jonah closed the shop with a note on the door that read Gone to see a lady about a clock, and he arrived at the cottage to find his grandfather already dressed. Daniel wore the good grey jacket that had been pressed twice, and he had combed his white hair flat with water, just as he had done on the day of the station. Jonah tied his tie for him, with great concentration, because his grandfather's fingers would not stop shaking, and he stood back to admire the result with the pride of a man who had finished a difficult repair.

Jonah's old blue van smelled of oil and peppermints, and it rattled along the coast road with all three of them squeezed into the front seat, Daniel in the middle with the biscuit tin on his knees. The sea flashed and vanished on their left as the road dipped and rose, and the sky was a pale and washed blue, as though the whole morning had been cleaned for the occasion. Nobody said much, but it was the sort of silence in which three people are all thinking about the same thing, and are glad of each other's company.

To steady his nerves Daniel began to hum, in a thin and slightly cracked voice, a slow waltz that he had not played, or sung, or even permitted himself to remember for years. He tapped the rhythm on the lid of the biscuit tin with one finger, and his eyes took on the faraway look of a man who was walking into a lantern-lit hall. After a few bars Iris closed her eyes and listened, and Jonah, who had never heard the tune before, found that he was driving in time to it.

Harbour View proved to be a long white house on a hill above the sea, with tall windows catching the morning sun and a wide, formal rose garden laid out at the front. The bushes were still bare in the cold air of late March, and the only colour on them was the first faint red of new leaves, pushing from the stems like small and hopeful flames. A gravel path ran between the beds to a glass door, and beside it a sign in neat green letters told visitors to ring the bell and sign the book.

Halfway along the gravel path Daniel stopped, quite suddenly, and the hand that held the biscuit tin began to shake so hard that the old letters rattled inside it. He whispered that he could not go in, because what if she did not want to see him, or saw him and was sorry? Iris took the tin gently from him and set it on a bench, and Daniel sat down beside it and stared at the roses as if they might offer him some advice.

Iris left the two men beside the roses, with Jonah's hand resting on his grandfather's shoulder, and went in alone with her heart thumping so loudly that she was sure it could be heard in the corridor. The hall smelled of floor polish and lilies, and at the front desk a kind young nurse glanced at the address inked on her hand, smiled, and said that Miss Ashby would be in the sun room. It was a long, quiet corridor lined with watercolours of the sea, and Iris walked down it as though she were crossing a bridge that might be taken away behind her.

The sun room was warm and bright, with tall windows that looked out over the sea and a row of armchairs arranged in friendly groups, most of them empty at that hour. In the last chair, beside the window, a small, upright woman with a cloud of white hair sat reading, her glasses on a chain around her neck and a library book open on her knee. She turned the page with a precise little movement, entirely absorbed, and Iris, standing in the doorway, felt that she was looking at someone she had known for years and was meeting for the very first time.

Iris crossed the room, asked in a voice that was not quite steady whether she was Miss Ruth Ashby, and held out the bundle of letters tied in her scarf. The woman looked up over her glasses with clear grey eyes that took Iris in from head to foot, and she said that she had been Miss Ruth Ashby for eighty-four years and was rather good at it. Then her gaze dropped to the scarf, and Iris saw the sharp, alert face begin, very slowly, to change.

Iris untied the scarf, and the blue ribbon lay in her palm, faded to the colour of a winter sky, and the old woman stared at it as though she were looking down a very long well. All the colour left her face, and her hand rose slowly to her throat, and for a moment Iris was afraid that she had made a terrible mistake. Then Ruth took the ribbon with a hand that trembled, pressed it against her cheek and began to laugh and cry at the same time, helplessly, like a girl of nineteen.

The drawer had stuck fast the very day that she hid the last letter, Ruth said when she could speak, and she had never managed to open it again, though she had always known exactly what lay behind it. She had been too ashamed to ask a carpenter for help, and too proud to break it, and so she had lived for sixty years with a secret she could neither share nor forget. When she moved here after her fall, her niece had cleared the flat in a hurry, and the old desk had gone to the saleroom, and Ruth had lain awake for weeks grieving for a piece of furniture.

For a while neither of them said anything, and the March sun lay in a warm square across the carpet between their chairs. Then Ruth wiped her eyes with the back of her wrist, sat up very straight, and asked, in a voice that had suddenly become small and formal, whether Iris happened to know what had become of Daniel Marsh. She asked it as if it were a question about the weather, and her fingers, tight around the faded ribbon, gave her away completely.

Iris knelt on the carpet beside the chair and took the old woman's free hand in both of hers, and said that yes, she did, and that he was not very far away at all. He was in the garden, she said, outside the glass door, sitting on a bench among the rose bushes with a biscuit tin full of letters of his own. Ruth drew one long breath, smoothed her white hair and her heather-coloured cardigan with fingers that would not keep still, and told Iris, with great composure, that she had better fetch him at once.

Iris ran out through the glass door and across the gravel, and she did not need to say a single word, because Jonah took one look at her face and helped his grandfather to his feet. Daniel walked up the corridor with one hand on her arm and the biscuit tin held to his chest, slowly, like a man crossing a river on stepping stones. At the doorway of the sun room he stopped, took off his cap, and stood there turning it round and round in his hands, a boy of eighty-six who had been sent for by the headmaster.

Ruth looked at him across the whole length of the sun room, at the white hair and the stoop and the kind, anxious eyes that had not changed in sixty-five years, and her face lit like a window at dusk. “You are late,” she said, in a voice that shook from end to end, and for a second Daniel could only stare at her. Then he began to laugh, helplessly, with the tears running down his face, and she laughed with him, and in the corner a very old gentleman woke up and wondered what he had missed.

He crossed the room, sat down beside her and took her hand in both of his, and for a long time neither of them said a word. At last Ruth took her final letter from the bundle in Iris's scarf, put on her glasses, and read it aloud in a clear, steady librarian's voice that faltered only once. At the last line, “If you ever come looking, I shall be waiting, and I shall not mind that you are late,” Daniel whispered that he had come as fast as he could.

Iris and Jonah stood side by side in the rose garden, looking at the tall window of the sun room, where two white heads could be seen bent close together over something small. A blackbird was singing somewhere in the bare bushes, and the sea lay flat and bright beyond the lawn, and it seemed to Iris that the whole world had stopped to hold its breath. Jonah said, in a low voice that was not quite steady, that he had never in his life seen his grandfather look so young.

They stood without speaking for a while, as people do when something larger than words has happened to someone they love, and then Jonah asked, rather shyly, what her own letter was waiting for. The question did not sound like a reproach; it sounded like the plain curiosity of a man who had watched her laugh and wondered what she kept locked away. Iris felt it land somewhere beneath her ribs, and slowly, as though her hand belonged to someone braver, she took her phone out of her pocket.

She opened the old draft to Pia, the one that had sat there for two years, and this time she did not read it through, because she knew that every line of it was wrong. It was long and careful and defensive, a letter written by a woman who wanted to be forgiven without having to ask for it, and she deleted it all with one long press of her thumb. In its place she wrote three plain lines, that she was sorry, that she missed her sister, and that she hoped they could talk, and her eyes were stinging as she did it.

Her thumb hovered above the little arrow for what felt like an hour, while the blackbird sang on in the rose bushes and the wind turned the pages of the visitors' book on a bench nearby. She thought of Ruth standing in a post office queue with an envelope held against her chest, and she thought, quite fiercely, not this time. Then she pressed send, and the message flew away with a soft, almost cheerful sound, and she felt sick and light at the same time, like a person who has stepped off a high wall.

They walked slowly round the rose beds, because it was impossible to stand still, and Jonah, with a tact she would remember for a long time, began to tell her about a customer whose clock ran backwards. It turned out, after three hours of investigation, that the customer had been holding it upside down, and Jonah told the story with such grave and detailed absurdity that she almost forgot to look at her phone. She did not forget for long, but she was grateful for every word, and she noticed that he never once glanced at the screen himself.

Her phone buzzed before they had even finished the second circuit of the roses, a short, sharp vibration that she felt in her teeth. Pia had answered at once, in less than a minute, and the message was so short that Iris read it twice before she could take it in. It said, “I have waited two years for this, so please call me, because Mum would be glad,” and Iris stopped in the middle of the path with the phone against her chest.

Iris read it twice, and then a laugh came out of her that turned, halfway through, into a sob, and she put the back of her hand against her mouth as if she could take it back. She had been so sure for two years that her sister was angry, and all that time her sister had been sitting at the other end of the silence, with her thumb over the same small button. Jonah, who had been standing very politely a few steps away, looking at the roses, produced from his pocket a clean handkerchief that smelled faintly of clock oil, and she laughed again and took it.

She rang her sister straight away, walking to the far end of the garden so that she could be alone with it, and for several seconds neither of them could say anything at all. Then Pia said her name, just once, in a voice that was thick and cracked and entirely familiar, and the two years between them seemed to shrink to the size of a hallway. They both began to say sorry at the same moment, and both stopped, and both began again, and then, to their astonishment, they both began to laugh.

When Iris and Jonah came back, Daniel had given Ruth the biscuit tin, and she sat with one of the four sealed envelopes unopened in her lap, her finger tracing the boyish handwriting of her old address. She told him then, simply and without excuses, why she had never posted a single letter, that she had been nineteen, and afraid, and ashamed of being afraid, and that every year of silence had made the next one heavier. Daniel listened without interrupting, and when she had finished he said, very gently, that he had never forgotten her, not for one day, and that he had been angry with nobody but himself.

She was glad, Ruth said, turning to Daniel, that he had married Margaret, because anyone who could keep a window open in her heart for a stranger must have been a very good woman indeed. Daniel's face crumpled and smoothed again, and he said that Margaret would have liked her, which was the greatest compliment he knew. Then Ruth turned to Iris and asked whether she would finish restoring the desk and bring it to her, because it belonged by a window, and so did she.

When visiting time came to an end, a nurse appeared in the doorway with a trolley and a tactful cough, and Ruth looked at the clock on the wall with open dismay, as though it had betrayed her. Daniel promised that he would come back on Saturday, and on the Saturday after that, and on every Saturday for as long as the staff would let him through the door. Ruth held on to his hand until the last possible moment, and then, with enormous dignity, she let it go, and lifted hers to wave.

It was dark by the time the blue van pulled away, and its headlights swept along the empty coast road in two pale, wavering tunnels, with the black sea breathing beyond the rail. Daniel was asleep before they had gone a mile, his head against the window and his cap in his lap, and his face in the glow of the dashboard looked as peaceful as a child's. Neither of the two awake in the van spoke, for fear of waking him, and the engine hummed on, and the lights of small villages slid past like a string of lanterns.

For a long time Jonah kept his eyes on the road, and when he spoke at last, it was in a low voice, quickly, as though he had been rehearsing the sentence since Saltmere. He asked whether she would have dinner with him, one evening, if he were to come up to the city, and he added, before she could answer, that it was entirely all right if she preferred not to. Iris looked out at the dark hedges flowing past, pretended to give the matter her most serious thought, and said that she believed she could probably be persuaded.

They stopped at the blue gate of Daniel's cottage, under the one streetlamp in the lane, and Jonah woke his grandfather with a gentle hand on his shoulder and helped him out into the cold. The old man stood swaying slightly, blinking at the stars, and then he took Iris's face between his hands, as if she were something very fragile and very precious, and kissed her on the forehead. He thanked her three times, in a voice that cracked on the third, and said that she had given him back a whole summer and that he did not know how he would ever repay her.

Jonah walked her up the steep hill to Mrs Dunmore's in the dark, and every few seconds the lighthouse beam passed over them, lighting the wet cobbles and the pale oval of his face before moving on out to sea. They did not talk much, but the silence was easy, and when they reached the blue door they both stopped at the same moment, as if they had been wound by the same key. He said goodnight, and she said goodnight, and then neither of them knew quite what to do with their hands, so they laughed, and she went in.

The next morning Jonah stood on the little platform to see her off, with his hands in his pockets and the wind in his hair, and Iris thought of another young man who had once stood in that very place. He did not try to hide that he was thinking of it too, and he said, with a quiet and perfectly steady smile, that he would ring every evening and that he had no intention of being late. Then the train came in, and Iris climbed aboard, knowing that this time the story would be different, because she was coming back.

As the train pulled out, she pressed her forehead against the cold glass and watched the little station shrink to a toy, with one tall figure on the platform still waving long after she could see him. The fields turned from green to brown and back again, the sea came and went on her left, and somewhere in the second hour she became aware that her face ached. It was only when a man across the aisle smiled at her, with the fond, indulgent look that people give to the very young and the very happy, that she realised she had been smiling since the harbour.

Back in the workshop, which smelled of dust and waiting after her two days away, she stood the oak desk under the lamp and began, with a scraper and solvent, to strip away the old polish. It was the part of her work that she loved best, because it demanded no cleverness, only attention, and because the wood seemed to sigh as the dull skin of a century came away. Layer by layer the grain came up under her hands, rich and golden and astonishingly alive, like a face that has been washed after a long journey.

Every evening at seven, as regular as one of his own clocks, her phone rang, and it was Jonah, with the sound of ticking just audible behind his voice. They talked about everything and nothing, about his customers and her varnish, about gulls and trains and what her sister had said, and neither of them ever wanted to be the first to say goodnight. Iris, who had spent two years composing messages that nobody read, found that she liked nothing better than to hear a voice reply.

The secret drawer was the first thing she mended, and she took more care over it than over the whole of the rest, because it was the one part of the desk that had nearly been lost for good. She planed the runners until they were as fine as silk, rubbed them with beeswax and slid the drawer in and out a dozen times, listening to the way it moved. It glided like a boat on still water, without a single catch, and Iris sat back on her heels, thinking of a girl who had pushed that same drawer shut for the last time.

Under the left-hand drawer, in a corner that no polish had ever reached, Iris found two small letters scratched into the wood with the point of a pin, R and A, very neat and slightly slanted. Beside them somebody had begun to cut a tiny heart and had then, apparently, been overcome by embarrassment, because it was half finished and had been rubbed with a thumb. Iris touched it with the tip of her finger and felt, across more than sixty years, the sudden hot loyalty of a person who has been shown a secret and has promised not to tell.

When the last polish was gone, the top of the desk showed a pale ring where a bottle of ink had stood, with a faint trail of drips like the tail of a comet. Iris could have sanded it away in a minute, as any restorer would have done, and nobody would have known the difference. But she looked at it for a long time, thinking of a girl bent over this very spot with a pen, and she decided that it was not a flaw but a signature.

On Saturday night Jonah told her over the phone, in a voice that was unusually soft, that Ruth had read Daniel's four old letters at last, with her glasses on and the tin open on her knee. They were short and shy and tender, he said, and each of them began with the same words, Dear Ruth, I hope you are quite well. She had read them aloud to his grandfather one after another, and at the end of the fourth, she had said that it was the most beautiful thing ever to have been returned to sender.

On the second Saturday a small green car pulled up outside the workshop, and Pia climbed out of it with a large cake tin held carefully in both arms, like a nurse carrying a baby. She stood in the doorway in her good coat, looking nervous and younger than Iris remembered, and said that she had not known what else to bring and that she hoped lemon was still all right. Iris, who had spent two years rehearsing what she would say if this moment ever came, found that she could say nothing whatever, and simply crossed the floor and put her arms around her sister.

They sat on the old sofa with tea and enormous slices of lemon cake, and for half an hour they talked about nothing in particular, as people do when they are building up the courage to land. Then Pia put down her fork, very deliberately, and said that she wanted to talk about the house. The workshop seemed to grow quiet around them, and even the radio in the corner, which was murmuring away as usual, had the grace to fall silent for a moment.

Pia admitted, with her eyes on her plate, that she had been frightened about money, more frightened than she had ever dared to say, and that she had hidden her fear behind a quarrel because anger felt easier to carry. Iris admitted that she had refused to listen, because she could not bear to lose their mother a second time, and that she had called her sister cold when she should have called her tired. By the end of it both of them were crying and laughing at once, and Pia was saying that they were pathetic, and Iris was saying that she had missed being insulted by somebody who knew her.

They agreed, at last and without a raised voice, that the house on Pell Road should be sold in the summer and the money shared fairly, which was what their mother would have wanted. They would keep her wooden chair, her tools and the old scrubbed kitchen table, which Pia had room for and Iris had always loved. And they would spend one last weekend in the house together, with the windows open and the kettle on, saying goodbye to it properly, which neither of them had been able to do alone.

Pia wandered over to the desk, which stood half restored under the lamp, and ran her fingertips along its edge with the unconscious tenderness of a woman who has grown up around wood. Iris told her the whole story from the beginning, the stuck drawer and the blue ribbon, the old man on the harbour wall and the old woman by the window, and Pia listened without interrupting. By the end of it she was wiping her eyes with a paper napkin and declaring that she meant to meet them both, and the clockmaker too, with a look that Iris could not quite read.

In the third week, on a cold bright evening, Iris rubbed the last coat of wax into the oak in slow circles, until the whole workshop smelled of beeswax and lavender. The desk glowed like honey under the lamp, deep and calm and handsome, and every scar and ink stain looked like a line in a story that was at last allowed to continue. She stood back and looked at it for a long time, and she thought that it was the finest thing she had ever restored, and that she had very little to do with it.

One evening, as she was cleaning her brushes and listening to the rain, the workshop door opened without a knock, and Jonah stood there on the threshold, out of breath and dripping, with his hair plastered flat. He was holding something against his chest, wrapped in a blue cloth, and he looked like a man who had run from the station, rehearsed a speech on the way and forgotten every word of it. Slowly, shyly, he unwrapped the cloth, and inside it was a small walnut clock, with a round white face and a tiny brass key, silent and perfect, like a very small heart waiting to begin.

Jonah hung the little clock on the wall above her workbench, with a borrowed nail and hammer, then set the hands with great concentration and wound the tiny brass key. It began to tick at once, softly and steadily, and the old workshop, which for years had held only sanding and sawing and the murmur of the radio, suddenly sounded like a place where somebody lived. Iris stood very still and listened, as one listens to a new voice in a familiar house, and found that she had a lump in her throat that she could not account for.

He told her, a little stiffly, that the clock had been silent on a back shelf for forty years, and that he had mended its battered case in the evenings, the way she had taught him. His ears were pink, and he spoke the way a man speaks who has practised, and who knows that the practice is about to fail him. It was for her, he finished, and he hoped, with a rush of honesty, that she would not mind the noise.

Then, before his courage could desert him, he asked whether she would have dinner with him that night, now, in whatever clothes she was wearing, if she was not too tired. Iris looked down at her stained overalls, with their ancient knees and their pockets full of screws, and burst out laughing, and said that she would need ten minutes and a hairbrush. She came back in a clean green shirt with her hair still damp, and Jonah, who had been studying the clock as though it were a masterpiece, turned round and forgot how to speak.

The restaurant on the corner was small and warm, with candles in old wine bottles on every table, steam on the windows and a large, cheerful man at the stove who sang under his breath. They were given the table at the back, by a radiator, and Jonah studied the menu with the frowning care he gave to a very difficult watch. Within ten minutes, helped by bread and olives and the plain kindness of a corner table, they had stopped being shy and had begun to talk as they had on the harbour wall.

Over the main course he confessed that he had never eaten in a city restaurant, and that he was a great deal more nervous than he looked, which Iris said was easy to see. He laughed, and then he stopped laughing, and his hand went inside his jacket and came out with something small and white and creased from being carried. He laid it on the tablecloth between the salt and the candle, slid it across with two fingers, and did not say a word.

It was an envelope with her name on the front in his small, careful handwriting, and it had clearly been in his pocket for weeks, because the corners were soft and grey. Inside was a single sheet, which began, Dear Iris, I have written this five times, and I have almost not sent it four of them. It went on for one page, plainly and without decoration, and what it said, in the end, was that since she had walked into his shop he had felt braver than he had ever been.

Iris read it twice, with one hand pressed to her mouth, while Jonah stared at the tablecloth as though he were hoping to find a small door in it and escape. Then she folded the page along its soft creases, pushed back her chair, walked round the table and put her hands on either side of his face. She kissed him, thoroughly and without the slightest embarrassment, in front of the waiters, the cook, the candles and an entire family at the next table.

For a moment the restaurant was perfectly silent, and then a small boy at the next table said, loudly, that they were kissing, and the whole room dissolved into laughter and applause. The large man at the stove turned round with his ladle in the air and bowed, as though the performance had been his own idea. A waiter arrived with a chocolate pudding, two spoons and a single candle, and announced, without a flicker of expression, that it came with the compliments of the house.

It was raining when they came out, a soft, silvery rain that hissed on the pavement, and they shared one black umbrella that was far too narrow for two people, let alone for their happiness. They walked slowly through the wet streets, their shoulders touching and their feet in all the puddles, and did not hurry, because neither of them wanted the evening to end. Somewhere near the canal Jonah asked, with elaborate casualness, whether she would take the desk to Ruth with him on Saturday, and she answered that she had already arranged to borrow a van.

At the workshop door she stopped, with the key in her hand and rain running down the back of her neck, and looked up at him in the yellow light of the streetlamp. For two years she had been a woman who composed the perfect sentence and never said it, and now she found that the perfect sentence was not necessary at all. She told him simply that she was very glad he had come, and that she intended to go on saying so, out loud, for as long as he would stand there and listen.

On Saturday morning Iris, Pia and Jonah wrapped the desk in thick blankets and carried it down the narrow stairs one careful step at a time, with Pia walking backwards and issuing instructions. Nobody spoke except to say left or lower or a little more, and the whole operation had the hushed solemnity of a state funeral conducted by amateurs. At last the desk slid into the back of the borrowed van without a single scratch, and the three of them stood in the street, panting and delighted, like people who have rescued something from a flood.

They drove for two hours along the coast road, with the desk strapped down in the back, Jonah at the wheel and Pia, wedged in the middle, talking cheerfully about everything she had ever thought of. Every time the van swung round a bend, Iris glanced over her shoulder at the blanketed shape behind them, as though it might have changed its mind. The sea went by on the left, enormous and blue and perfectly indifferent, and the day was so clear that she could see the gulls' shadows moving on the water.

Daniel was waiting at the gate of Harbour View in his best grey jacket, with a bunch of yellow daffodils in one hand and the other hand resting on the gate-post like a man holding himself upright by willpower. He had come on the early train, he said, because he had not slept, and he had been standing there since nine, watching the road for a blue van that turned out to be a white one. When he saw the blanketed shape in the back of the van, he took off his cap and held it to his chest, as if a procession had passed, and laughed at himself.

Four of them carried the desk down the long corridor, past a row of curious faces at every open door, and an old man in a dressing gown who saluted it gravely as it went by. At the far end, in a sunny room that looked out over the roses and the sea, a nurse had already cleared the corner beneath the window and put a jug of water on the sill for Daniel's daffodils. They set the desk down in its place with the care of people laying a sleeping child in a cot, and straightened up, and there was a small silence.

Ruth, who had been waiting in her armchair as straight as a ruler, rose with the help of her stick and crossed the room very slowly, as if the desk might vanish if she hurried. She laid her palm flat on the polished oak, and then her forefinger found the pale ring left by a bottle of ink sixty years before, and she traced it round, once, twice, and a third time. When Iris showed her the two small letters under the drawer and the half-finished heart, Ruth made a sound that was part laugh and part sob, and said she had been nineteen and ridiculous, and was glad.

Then Iris showed her the secret drawer, and Ruth, with one finger, slid it open, smooth and silent as a breath, and looked into the empty space behind it where sixty years of her silence had lain. There was nothing there at all now but clean pale wood and the faint scent of beeswax, and Ruth gazed into it for a long moment with an expression that Iris could not read. It was wonderful, she said at last, to look into that dark little place and find that it had nothing to hide.

Daniel, who had been holding himself in with visible effort, now produced a brown paper bag and laid out on the desktop a pad of cream paper, a packet of envelopes and a book of stamps. He had bought them on Thursday at the post office in Saltmere, he explained, from a girl who had asked whether he was starting a business. Every one of those stamps, he said, with the solemnity of a man swearing an oath, was for a letter that would be posted.

Ruth took her old fountain pen from her cardigan pocket and wrote Dear Daniel at the top of a clean sheet, in the same slanting hand that Iris had first seen in March. Daniel sat in the armchair beside the window, with a tray across his knees, and began a letter of his own, tongue between his teeth, like a boy at school. For ten whole minutes neither of them spoke, and the only sounds in the sunny room were the scratch of two pens and the faint sea-breath of the wind at the glass.

When both letters were sealed and stamped, Ruth and Daniel took each other's arm and walked out through the glass door, with Iris, Pia and Jonah following at a respectful distance. The red post box stood at the gate, as plain and solid as a sentry, and for a moment the two of them stood in front of it without moving, looking at the black slot. Then Ruth let her letter fall, and Daniel let his fall after it, and they listened to the two soft sounds of paper landing, and Ruth said, very quietly, that it was the loveliest noise she had ever heard.

The visit ended at four, as visits do, and the three of them went out to the van, leaving the two old people at the window of the sunny room, beside the desk. Ruth waved, with the faded blue ribbon looped around her fingers like a bracelet, and Daniel stood close behind her, already arguing, with great happiness, about whose letter would reach the other first. Iris, looking back through the rear window at the two small figures in the golden light, thought that she had never seen two people look less like a secret.

One bright morning in April, Ruth informed the staff of Harbour View, with the calm of a general announcing a campaign, that she intended to live in Saltmere again, if somebody would be so good as to help her. The doctor frowned, the matron sighed, and a physiotherapist was summoned to assess how far she could walk, and she walked, with her stick and her chin well up, the entire length of the corridor and back. By the end of the week all three had agreed, for the simple reason that nobody could remember having seen anyone want anything so clearly.

Jonah, who had never searched for anything faster than a missing screw, found within four days a small whitewashed cottage near the lighthouse, with a blue door and a south-facing window that looked straight out to sea. Its owner, who turned out to be a cousin of Mrs Dunmore, said that she would be delighted to let it to someone who would love it, and named a rent so modest that Ruth suspected a conspiracy. Daniel inspected the place from top to bottom with a clockmaker's eye, pronounced the roof sound and the stairs honest, and wiped, with one finger, a speck of dust from the windowsill that had no business being there.

Ruth spent a week packing, with the concentration of a woman who has had sixty years to decide what matters. She chose her books one by one, giving most of them to the home's library with a handwritten note in the front of each, and keeping only the twenty that she could not do without. Into the same small suitcase went her glasses, her cardigans, a photograph of her mother, and, wrapped in a woollen scarf, the old biscuit tin with its four faded envelopes.

Moving day came in late May, on a morning so clear and still that the sea looked as if it had been painted on glass. Jonah drove the blue van, with the desk roped in the back, and Ruth sat beside him in her hat and gloves, holding her handbag on her knees like a person on her way to an interview. At every turn of the coast road she leaned forward a little, and when the lighthouse came into view she put one gloved hand flat against the windscreen, as if to be sure that it was real.

After lunch Ruth announced that she would walk the harbour wall to the lighthouse, and that anyone who suggested a wheelchair would be sent home. She took her stick in one hand and Daniel's arm in the other, and they set out between the nets and lobster pots at a pace that would have shamed a snail, while the fishermen watched with great respect. It took them half an hour, with three stops to look at the sea, and at the foot of the white tower Ruth laid her cheek against the warm stone and said that it had been worth the wait.

That evening, when the desk had been set down under the cottage window, with its face to the sea, Ruth sat down at it as though she had never been away. The ink ring lay under her left hand, and the lamp on the lighthouse was just beginning to turn behind the glass, throwing its slow beam across the water and, every few seconds, across her sleeve. She wrote the date at the top of a clean page, uncapped her pen, and began a letter to Daniel, who lived exactly three streets away and who would be knocking at her door within the hour.

On Monday morning she walked the length of Quay Street on her stick and pushed open the door of Marsh and Son, and the little brass bell rang exactly as it had rung in August 1961. She stood very still among the ticking clocks with her eyes half closed, as if she were listening to a piece of music she had learned long ago, and Jonah, behind the counter, had the good sense to say nothing. Then she crossed the shop, laid her hand flat on the worn wood where a young man had once opened a stopped watch, and said that it had hardly changed at all.

A few days later, over tea and a plate of Mrs Dunmore's shortbread, Ruth told Iris about her life, and she told it without sentiment, the way she might have catalogued a collection. She had been a librarian for forty years, and she had loved nearly all of them, because a library is a place where nobody is in a hurry and every question is allowed. She had never married, she said, not out of sorrow but out of a kind of plain loyalty to a room in her own heart, and she had been, on the whole, rather content.

Her only real regret, she said, was a single drawer and what she had put in it, and it had taken a stranger with a thin blade to show her how much that silence had cost. She opened the drawer in question, which now slid out as softly as water, and took from it her old black fountain pen, with its worn gold nib, which she had not let out of her sight since March. Then she put it into Iris's hand and folded her fingers around it, firmly, with the cool dry strength of a woman who had spent a lifetime stamping books.

“Do not keep your words in a drawer, my dear,” she said, and her grey eyes were suddenly very bright, “because they are no use to anyone until they are sent.” She told her to say the thing while there was someone to hear it, and to say it badly if she must, because a clumsy sentence that arrives is worth more than a perfect one that does not. “And if you ever stand before a post box with your heart in your mouth,” she added, with the ghost of a smile, “think of an old woman who would be exceedingly cross with you.”

In June a letter arrived from her landlord, written in the careful, regretful language of people who are about to sell a building, and it informed Iris that the lease on her workshop would end in September. She read it three times at the bench, with the new clock ticking above her head, and waited for the familiar sinking feeling of a woman whose plans have been taken from her. It did not come, and she realised, with a small shock, that what she felt was not dismay but a kind of astonished and slightly guilty relief.

She told Pia over the phone that evening, in a careful voice, and Pia, who had never been careful in her life, said at once that of course she must go to Saltmere. Iris had never been so happy, Pia said, as when she talked about that town, and she added that she would visit every month, whether Iris liked it or not. Iris laughed, and felt something that had been clenched inside her for two years let go, quite quietly, like a hand that has finally been given permission to open.

On her next visit, walking along Quay Street with a paper bag of shortbread, Iris noticed a To Let sign propped in the window of an empty shop, two doors along from Marsh and Son. The glass was grey with dust and a dead moth lay on the sill, but the window was tall and wide, and it faced north, towards the cold clear light that every restorer longs for. She stood on the pavement with her nose almost against the glass, and felt the odd, quiet, certain feeling of having come to the right door after a long walk.

The landlord, a Mr Pascoe, turned out to be a small, round, anxious man with an enormous ring of keys, and he unlocked the door with a flourish and a warning that the lock was temperamental. Inside, dust turned slowly in long bars of sunlight, and the room rose to a high ceiling with a plaster rose at its centre, above a floor of worn grey flagstones. At the back was a second room with a sink and a stove, a yard with a lemon tree in a tub, and a flight of stairs leading to two bright rooms that looked out over the harbour.

Iris stood in the middle of the stone floor and turned slowly round, seeing the long benches under the window, the racks of clamps and the chairs waiting in a patient row. The north light came through the tall glass soft and even and without a single hard shadow, the kind of light in which you can see exactly what a piece of wood is thinking. She told Mr Pascoe, in a voice that wobbled only a little, that she would take it, and he looked so relieved that she suspected nobody else had asked.

That evening she told Jonah, in the clock shop, and for a moment he simply stood there with his mouth a little open, as though a wheel somewhere inside him had slipped a tooth. Then he crossed the floor in two strides, lifted her off her feet as if she weighed nothing, and spun her round, laughing, until the old clocks on the top shelf began to chime in confusion. When he set her down, they were both out of breath, and the oldest clock of all, which had not struck in living memory, solemnly struck thirteen.

Jonah painted the sign himself, with a fine brush and a steady hand, a dark green board with gold capitals that read Calloway, Furniture Restorer, and underneath, in smaller letters, Begun This Year. Daniel supervised from a kitchen chair set on the pavement, with his cap tilted against the sun, and offered a running commentary on the lettering that Jonah received with perfect good humour. When the paint was dry, the three of them lifted it onto its bracket above the door, and it caught the evening light and shone like a small, hopeful lighthouse of its own.

In August the village hall held its summer dance, as it had done for a hundred years, with paper lanterns in yellow, green and rose strung from beam to beam. The whole of Saltmere seemed to be there, in its best clothes, and the air smelled of floor polish and lemonade and the sea. Ruth arrived on Daniel's arm in a new blue dress, with her stick, and in her white hair, fastened with a small, careful bow, the old blue ribbon that she had worn on the night when she was nineteen.

When the band struck up the same slow waltz, Daniel rose from his chair, stood in front of Ruth as straight as his years allowed, and offered her his arm with a small, courtly bow. She hooked her stick over the back of a chair, took his hand, and the two of them moved out onto the floor beneath the lanterns, slowly, carefully and in perfect time. The whole hall fell quiet, and then began, one pair of hands after another, to applaud, and the sound rose to the beams like a flock of startled birds.

Jonah, who had been standing by the lemonade table with the expression of a man contemplating a cliff, finally crossed the floor and asked Iris to dance, and within three steps he had trodden firmly on her foot. He stopped dead and went scarlet, apologising in a rush, and Iris, who had been steeling herself for the pain, began instead to laugh so helplessly that she had to hold on to his sleeve. She managed to say at last that now she understood why the story was told in his family, and that she would not have had him any other way.

On a warm evening in late summer the four of them sat in a row on the harbour wall, with their legs dangling over the water and a bag of shortbread being passed from hand to hand. The sun went down behind the lighthouse in a long smear of gold and rose, and the tide came in slowly beneath them, patting the stones as if it wished to be asked to stay. Iris looked along the row of faces, the white head, the old cap, the shy sidelong smile, and thought, with perfect certainty, that there was nowhere else in the world that she would rather be.

Ruth took a letter from her handbag and read it aloud with the briskness of a librarian, a short and rather funny note from Daniel that the postman had delivered that morning. Daniel pretended to be mortified, and put his cap over his face, but he was smiling so widely beneath it that the gulls edged closer to find out what was the matter. Jonah laughed until he had to wipe his eyes, and Iris, watching Ruth's proud, upright profile against the sky, thought that it was the finest piece of correspondence that she had ever heard.

When the light had nearly gone, Iris said as lightly as she could that she would have to go back to the city one last time, to pack up the workshop and hand over the keys. Jonah at once offered to come and carry the heavy things, but he had already understood that she was going to say no. It was something she wanted to finish by herself, she told him, as gently as she could, so that she could arrive in Saltmere with nothing left behind her.

Pia arrived on Thursday in her oldest jeans, with a flask of coffee and six rolls of tape, and the two sisters worked side by side for two days, wrapping clamps and brushes in newspaper. Whenever one of them found something that belonged to their mother, a pencil stub or a faded apron, she held it up in silence, and the other nodded, and into the keep box it went. In the last drawer they found the little wooden plane, worn smooth by decades of use, and Pia put it into Iris's hands and said, in a thick voice, that it belonged in the new shop.

By Friday evening the van was packed to the roof, and the workshop, swept and echoing and strangely large, looked like a room that has been told a secret and is waiting politely to be left alone. Pia hugged her until her ribs creaked, promised to be in Saltmere on Sunday with the kitchen table, and drove away in her little green car with her hand out of the window, waving, until she turned the corner. Iris went back inside, locked the door behind her and stood in the middle of the bare floor, listening to the walnut clock, the last thing on the wall, ticking in the silence.

She sat down at the bare bench where she had spent so many nights, on the one stool that she had left until last, and took from her pocket the old black fountain pen with its worn gold nib. In front of her lay a single clean sheet of her best cream paper, and for a long time she did nothing at all but look at it. The clock ticked, and the pen lay in her hand as light as a feather and as heavy as a promise.

Then she began to write, slowly at first, and then faster, in a hand that was not at all neat, the words that she would never have dared to say aloud on the harbour wall. She wrote that she was afraid, that she had spent years being afraid, and that being near him had made her feel that fear was a coat she could take off. She wrote that she was happier than she had ever been, that the shop was not only about the light, and that she loved him, plainly and entirely, and was not going to be ashamed of saying so.

She read it through once, without changing a word, which was a thing she had never done in her life, and folded it in three along the creases that her fingers seemed to know already. Then she slid it into an envelope, wet the flap with the tip of her tongue and pressed it shut, and wrote on the front, in careful capitals, Jonah Marsh, Marsh and Son, Quay Street, Saltmere. The stamp was the last thing she needed, and she took it from the book that Daniel had pressed into her hand at the dance, and smoothed it onto the corner with her thumb.

She switched off the lamp, took the walnut clock from its nail and tucked it under her arm, and stepped out into a night that smelled of rain and warm pavements. The street was dark and quiet, with the lamps making small yellow pools on the ground, and the only sound was her own footsteps and, from the clock against her ribs, a faint and steady ticking. At the corner stood the red post box, solid and patient, and she walked towards it with the letter held tightly in her hand, as another young woman had once walked a very long time ago.

She held the letter above the dark mouth of the box for a long moment, with the whole of the summer standing behind her, and then she let it go and listened to it fall. Then she turned back towards the empty workshop, with the clock ticking against her ribs, knowing that by this time tomorrow she would be in Saltmere, where a lamp that had never once failed would be turning. The letter would arrive a day after she did, which was perfectly foolish, but she had learned from a stranger's drawer that some words are worth nothing until they are sent.
